him; but I am rather puzzled. 1 must acumr, as to his actual identity. I wired the head of the Bavarienburg police this morning as to Prince Rudolph's whereabouts, expecting to hear that he was ' away ' or ill,' but he tele- graphed back that he was at the Castle and had been, without intermission, for some weeks."
"Humph 1 that's strange," Ladmitted the Home Secretary: " but we must see whethet this 'Mr. Stuart' has fled back home, or whether he is someone else."

Sir Hugo took his leave: and the Minister tried to focus his attention upon other less exciting work, but failed utterly. He could do nothing but thinkof the affairs of the day and wonder what the next few hours would bring forth. Suddenly he looked up at the clock and saw that it was a quarter past five. "I'm doing no good here," he murmured to himself. " I may as well be off." He put on his heavy coat and went down- stairs in a preoccupied state of mind. In the doorway he halted for a moment. "My carriage, Jennings," he said to the commissionaire: and he stood in the doorway buttoning up his gloves, while the man called it up. "I wonder they never had a go for me," he was thinking to himself, "considering how useful the run of the Home Office would have been to them. Thank goodness they won't have the chance now."

Suddenly a dark form sprang forward out of the shadow of the night, appearing from no- where, as it were, and a revolver rang out sharply through the crisp air. Mr. Colgate felt a shock and staggered back into the doorway, falling prostrate in the hall of the Home Office.

His assailant, with a maniacal light in his blood-shot eyes, began to ascend the steps as fast as a lame leg would allow, but Jennings was too quick for him. However, before the old tsoldier could seize him, the murderer, hearing his approach, jumped to one side and, putting the barrel of the revolver into his own mouth, pulled the trigger a second time. An hour later the papers were selling for a shilling a piece in the West End, as they con- tained a vivid account of how Lord Branksea, the heir to the marquisate of Swanage, had shot the Home Secretary through the brim of his hat and subsequently committed suicide
by blowing out ms own Drams. It was the biginning of the end of the " White Rose ti conspiracy.
(To be continued.)

THE . . .
WHITE ROSE.
By GERALD BISS,
CHAPTER XXXll.—Continue4
A dreadful silence fell upon them both, as they stood gazing into each other's white face.

At last the duke took a step forward and clasped his wife's hand. "My darling, my poor darling," he mur- mured hoarsely. To think that it should come to this alter all these years I " "Don't blame yourself, dear husband," she said with unusual softness in her voice. "It's mainly my fault; and we must be brave and pay for—for our big mistake." Without a word he took her in his great arms and held her close to him. Then he kissed her 'passionately on the lips and released her.

" I must tell the others," he said more calmly. "You, dear, find Lady Swanage, Lady Mary, Mrs. Mackenzie and Mrs. Mclver and bring them here. I'll find the men. We must settle something before lunch. Within a few minutes they had all fore- gathered, pale at knowledge of some grave tidings. "It is no time to mince words, ladies and gentlemen," said the duke, holding up his hand for silence. "In a word, the game is up, and we are all in danger of arrest, I fear. How much is actually known, or how many names arc in the hands of the police, I do not know: but these wires explain themselves." Calm again, and speaking in his most im- perturbable manner, he read the three tele- grams in a cold, level voice, which drove home their meaning to every heart in the room, striking them chill. Then he went on speaking. "The duchess and I are going up to town by the three o'clock train; and there will be a meeting to-night at eight in the usual place. That is for those who care to attend it, as I feel that the. committee must now be con- sidered dissolved, bound together only by the secrets which affect us all so nearly. Each must act for himself and use his own judg- ment. The only difect evidence, so far as I know, depends upon Lord Ben Nevis, whose life still hangs by a thread; but I have no doubt that the police have or will have a pretty good inkling of all the names, even if they lack evidence to convict. I should ad- vise those of you who. value your lives and • think that you have a chance of escape, to make direct for Southampton and the Con- tinent by that route. Those whom Ben Nevis is certain to remember as ringleaders had better accompany the duchess and myself to town and hold a consultation. I shall tele- graph to the others to meet me one by one this afternoon before the last conunittee meeting of the 'White Rose.'" The duke sat down, drawing his hand across his forehead as though bored and tired of the whole affair. An hysterical groan came from Mrs. Mc- Iver. "I shall go -abroad for a time, I think," she sobbed, clutching the arm of Atherley, who was next to her. A grim smile seemed to flicker for an instant round his usually imperturbable mouth. " I shalt go to town with you, sir," he said, bowing to his host. "I, too," said Colonel Mclver, coolly. " And I," said Portcullis thickly. sooner it's over the better." " I'm for town, too." said Branksea with a strange glitter in his eyes, " and a last din ' Then the Marchioness of Swanage spoke. "Lord Swanage and I will accompany you, duke," she said in a clear, unemotional voice. Her husband, more apopleptic than eves with excitement, acquiesced unwillingly. " There's no way out of it, it seems," he, said plaintively, as though grumbling at fate. "No," said Lord Stepney in a dull voice; and Lord Struan nodded without a word. Then Lady Mary Renfrew spoke. " I shall not desert the cause. I'm too old to turn disloyal." "I shall come to town," said Ellis Gordon enigmatically. Mr. Stuart Mackenzie and his wife had been whispering in a low tone. " I—l think we'll go abroad, too," he said at length in a quavering voice. "No one will remember us: and it's better to live in—in Spain or--or--" "Anywhere else," broke in Fllis Gordon abruptly, "than to die in London, isn't it I doubt if, being a political conspiracy, they could extradite you, even if they took the trouble to try." "I'm corning to town, sir, of course," said the Master of Gareloch. "No, you are not, my dear boy," answered the duke sharply. "I won't have it. It is unlikely that Ben Nevis saw you, even if he lives to tell the tale,: and it's not worth your while sacrificing your life; when there's no need. That's foolhardiness, not pluck. Your punishment will be exile. I should advise the Colonies to a young fellow like you and a fresh start." "Thank you, sir," said the young Scotsman sadly ;" I suppose you are right. But I hate taking your advice. Mrs. Mclver was arguing hysterically with her husband in a corner. "Your first duty, Mclver, is to your wife," said the duke, laying his hand on the other's shoulder. "You'll do no good by corning to town, and I doubt if the King will wish any
!I Tht

steps taken so long as a sufficient number pair the penalty and the rest do not return. Re- /member, the proofs against most of you are very slight, if indeed such at all as would rank in law, and depend solely upon Ben Nevis' recovery. I intend, also, to entrust my cleat old friend, Lady Mary, to your care, whether she wishes it or not." The old lady made an indignant motion of protest; but the duke took her hand in hiS gently, but firmly. " Dear friend, I insist," he said in a low voice. "You will take a great weight off my mind by doing so. I want as few as possible to suffer." _ _ .

" If you ask me, I yield; but I hate it," said the loyal old lady tremulously pressing his hand. "But it will not be for long now." • He bent over and kissed the hand he held. She had been his mother's dearest friend, and 'he had loved her ever since he could remem- ber. "Now, my dear," he said, turning to the duchess, who was standing by his side with a look of admiration in her eyes as she watched 'his cool manner and masterful bearing, " to lunch at once; and then we must dissolve the party or leave them in Charlie's hands. We must not forget to send the news of the post- ponement to the village. I'm afraid it will upset them terribly."

div.head: CHAPTER XXXIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXIII.

IT was nearly one o'clock before Sir Huge Verschoyle could find time to get round tc Half Moon Street to inquire after Ben Nevi., and interview Bina. He was sorry for the girl with a sorrow toc deep for expression, but in the excitement and turmoil of the intervening twelve hours he had scarcely had time to give her a thought. But, above all, it made him intensely miser- able to think that in no way would his duty Allow him to lighten the awful blow which must fall on her and leave its mark on her whole life. " The sins of the fathers again," he mur- mured, as he drove round. "It has always seemed so illogical and unfair to me 1" At the door the inspector • met him with a grave face. Lord Ben Nevis is better," he said in answer to his chief's questions, "but Lady Sabina seems frightfully ill, and the doctors Lear brain fever. She came down this morn- Mg between ten and eleven, white and hag. gard, and seemed like a person in a trance. She had her hat on and went straigat oui without a word to anyone." " Went out ? " ejaculated Sir Huge abruptly. 14 Yes, sir, she went out walking and re- -turned within half an hour in a cab. Ttw
constable on duty helped her out as she could, hardly stand. In the hall she fell all of a flog anl hasn't recovered consciousness yet. Dr. Sholto is with her now and seems very anxious."

The head of the police frowned as he passed through the hall to the sitting-room. "Loyal till death despite all," he muttered. " I might have known it. She has wired some sort of a warning to Southsea Castle. I'll send a code-wire to .Mullins down there to warn him to look out for developments." In the sittiag-room he found the nurse and asked for Lady Grizelle.
She entcrea a moment later, pale and anyzia-a.s.

" Dina b ill," she said hurriedly, "and I can't stop. Dr. Sholto fears brain fever. He says she must have had some terrible shock on top .of everything else. Do you know what it wa,t ? " Sir 111:1,..) bowed gravely.

"/ cannot tell you now, I'm afraid," he said s.1:117 ; " but you will learn for yourself all too s,;111." slArly Grizelle was too much a woman of the world to press the point, mysterious as it all was to her.
"I am not ~;ufft that I ought not to wire to South.,qn CAstle," she went on ; "but there is the Ei:l:;'s visit."

"Ii Maje.ity will not go to Southsea Castle to-day," said the chief of the detective depa rtruPnt. " There are grave develop ments pending, and he is required at Wind- sor." Lady.Crizelle looked puzzled.
" Sh-all I wire then' 4
" Wait a few hours. I shall hope to call again this evening. And Lord Ben Nevis? How is he? " " No worse, if not better; and the doctors hope he will live, though it's still touch and go.:

She took his hand as he said, good-bye. " Don! t keep me in suspense too long, Sir Hugo, I pray you. Your words have made me strangely anxious." " Not a minute longer than I can help, dear lady," he said, pressing her hand sympa- thetically, and he went away deeply touched.
At thi.ee o'clock be ,was at the IHome Office to kcep his appointment. - • . He was shown straight into Mr.. Colgate's room and found him alone, 'looking terribly worried.
"Any news ? " the Home Secretary asked anniously.

" 'expecting wires here every minute," answered Verschoyle ; " but 1 have taken no steps vet, as arranged. The Ring's illness and the postponement Of the visit to Southsea Castle are announced in the evening papers and are causing A tremendous stir, as you may imagine.' People are talking of nothing else and speculating as • to. ivhether he may not be more seriously ill than is stated. Lady Sabina Belsize is, I fear, down with brain fever," went on the detective, " at least, so the doctors think."
"Poor girl," said the Home Secretary gravely. The icing was very concerned about her."

"She is grit all through. This morning, when she was not fit to stand, she went and, I fancy, sent her father a wire to warn him of the discovery of the plot. Then she dropped down like a dead woman."

" Humph," muttered the Cabinet Minister, " that's aiding and abetting,it seems to me." " It's only natural," rejoined the other warmly; "but that's another question. Lord Ben Nevis' on the other hand, is doing as well as can be expected, and the doctors hope that now he may pull through. He's essential to the case, it seems to me, as he is the only direct evidence. But how did the King take it ? " " Like myself," replied Mr. Colgate, "at first he refused to believe it possible; but he realised that it was hardly likely that I should demand a personal interview so abruptly on a wild-goose chase, or suggest such a drastic change in his plans without a solid reason. And after he had gone into your statement he uow SC/lOUS II was. a o say that he was upset and grieved is a mild word, and he asked me to leave him for a short time to collect his thoughts. When I was sum- moned again into the royal presence I found his Majesty quite calm and collected, and he discussed the matter with me in all its befirings. At first he Was anxious to avoid a public scandal for the sake of the nation, showing at the same time more consideration for his old friends who had turned traitors, than they had shoWn for him. Then he realised that such a course would be nothing short of condoning the most horrible series of murders the country has ever seen ; and that on grounds of public morality alone it would be impossible. At last he agreed that the ring- leaders should be arrested to-night; but his desire is that such of the small fry of the con- spiracy as care to escape in the meantime shoud not be followed up so long as they remain out of the country. I pointed out to him the statement in your note that the burden of the proof rested Inainly upon Lord Ben Nevis's evidence; and that whereas he might die, even if he lived, it was unlikely that he would be able to identify by any means all the con- spirators. So his -Majesty's final decision was that we should issue writs against them all, but only execute them in the case of those who remained in the country or returned to it. It is now certain that the whole affair will ultimately have to become public property, so that any who flee now are scarcely ever likely to re- turn. Now what do you propose to do with regard to arresting the leading conspirators ?" ' I am expecting to have a wire from Mullins at any moment acquainting me with the movements of the house-party at South- sea Castle, and I shall base my course of action upon that. Of course, the King consented at once to postpone his visit and keep to his apartments ? " Naturally ; the moment he was con- vinced of the existence of the plot and its serious nature. He made Sir kilan Kitcat telegraph at noon." At that moment a knock came on the door, and a messenger entered with a telegram. "For you." skid the Home Secretary, ;landing it to Sir Hugo, who tore it opesa.l "Duke, duchess, Swanages, Branksea, Stepney, Strnan, Portcullis, Atherley and Gordon left for town by 3.5 train. Duke sent batch of wires on way to station. Am staying to watch rest of party and will wire Yard,later. Royal wire arrived 12.17; immense sensation in neighbourhood. Previously two wires fps castle. Fancy others may be going Saudi ampton 5.40. Waiting instructions.— Mou.ms." •
Verschoyle read it aloud. " May I use your telephone ? " he asked. "I want to speak to the Yard." The Home Secretary nodded; and he was on in an instant. - --

"Is that you, Montgomerie ? Oh, all right. Detail two smart men to meet Hamp- shire train in at Waterloo 4.50, and shadow the Duke of Hampstead. They are to make no arrests, but to report movements. Send two others to watch Hampstead House, Bel- grave Square, and two mote to watch the duke's house on the Heath. I shall be round I shortly myself: but act at once. You under- stand clearly? All right. Good-bye." When he had rung off he wrote a wire to Mul- lins. "Wire developments Yard. Make no arrests, and do not impede flight if attempted. —VERSCHOYI.t." -

" Only the small fry left," he said to the Home Secretary. "and we have practically no evidence awainst them beyond the graves* suspicion. We can afford to dispense with them, espe—lally as it is the King's wish. I fancy there will be a meeting of the ring- leaders to-night, judging by the duke's batch of wires; and I'll surround the house and take those that are left then. Now I must be off to make my srlangements." "Yes, so far so good," agreed the Home Secretary. "If we can get the ringleaders only it will be best. By file way, be careful of this mysterious 'Mr. Stuart,' if you arrest him. If he turns out to be Prince Rudolph of Bavarienburg, we shall have to deport hitt" quietly to save compllcations. You under- stand? Arrest him by all means, but keep it dark." "Yes, I understand." said Verschoyle. I had intended to consult you first if we caught

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE. "
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE. "
MORE SECONDARY SCHOOL ACCOMM9DATION NEEDED.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee was held at the Town Hall on Monday even- ing, Alderman Bennett presi line. Thero were also present:—the Mayor(Alderman Bolton),the Revs. Canon Morley Stevenson and Father Wilson, Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Brough, Sankey, Fulton-Smith, Evans, Wilkinson, Wright, Burton, and Lord, Messrs. H. Roberts, A. J. Jolley, 11„ T. Fairclongh, E. Plinston, J. Upson, G. Walker, T. May, W. Bibby, J. Moore Murray (secretary and director), and J. Fairhurst (treasurer and accounting officer).

THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL. The CllainmaNexpressed gratification that the Coun- cil unanimously confirmed the new scheme with refer ence to the Grammar School. He trusted that the institution would have a long career of prosperity before it. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: BEAMONT SCHOOL.
div.p: THE BEAMONT SCHOOL.

A letter was submitted to the Finance Committee from the Town Clerk enclosing a copy of a communica- tion received from the Local Government Board for- warding their sanction to the loan for the erection of the " Beamont " Council school, together with an extract from the proceedings of the Sites and Buildings Committee at their meeting on the Bth December, 1905, calling the attention of this Committee to the period allowed by the Board for the repayment of the loan (29 years) which, in the opinion of that Committee, is insufficient. It was resolved, that a representation be made to the Local Government Board with a view, if possible, to an extension of that period being allowed. The minutes were approved. THE TRAINING OF PUPIL TEACHERS.

In moving the adoption of the School Management Committee's minutes, Canon Morley Stevenson alluded to the fact that representatives of the Com- mittee (Mr. C. E. Parker and the director) attended a conference held at Bradford on the subject of the education of pupil teachers. There seemed to be an impression gaining ground that the Board of Education did not favour the retention of pupil teachers' centres but preferred that the education of pupil teachers should be given solely in Secondary schools. Certain towns had gone to great expense in the building and equipment of pupil teachers' centres, and consequently they were rather alarmed at the attitude of the Board of Education. At the conference there was a unanimity of opinion that all pupil teachers should receive a good secondary education up to the age of sixteen years but there was a little differ- ence of opinion as to whether the training of pupil teachers should be given in Secondary

'schools or at the pupil teachers' centres. The conference unanimously adopted a resolution asking the Board to allow considerable latitude to local educa- tion authorities as to the retention of pupil teachers' centres. A resolution was also passed expressing the opinion that it was desirable that more assistance should be given from the Imperial Exchequer to educa- tion and that such assistance should take the form of making the training of pupil teachers al national charge. THE SECONDARY SCHOOL. MORE ACCOMMODATION WANTED.

At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter, dated the 30th November, was submitted from the Board of Education, intimating that the secondary school had been placed on the list of schools recognized under the regulations for secondary schools for the year 1905-6 and that the Board were prepared to accept the existing scale of fees charged providing the fee was forthwith made annual or terminal, to be paid in advance, and suggesting that the fee should be inclusive of charges for games, materials, Ac., and that a formal undertaking should be required from the parents that their children would remain at the school for the full period for which they were admitted. It was resolved , that from the Ist August, 1906, the fees to be charged for scholars of the secondary school be lOs. 6d. per term or 30s. per annum : and that resolution No. C 105 (a) be amended accordingly. The reportiof the sub-committee appointed to con- sider the report from the Board of Education upon the recent inspection of the Secondary School was sub- mitted, and, with a view to meeting the comments con- tained therein, it was decided that the following ladies be invited to act as a Visiting and Advisory Com- mittee, viz. :—Miss White, of Holly House, gankey- street, Mrs. Edelsteu, of Norton Lodge, Norton, and Mrs. Stevenson, of the Training College, Warrington ; that the Education Committee be responsible for the provision of a playing field for the scholars attending the Secondary School ; that, if possible arrangements be made for the scholars to attend the baths during the iumtner months ; that arrangements be made for the wife of the caretaker to prepare and warm the food of those scholars who do not go home to dinner ; that a small charge be made upon the scholars for this service; and that the headmaster be instructed to arrange for the teachers to undertake the supervision of the scholars in question • and that a sub-committee, con- sisting of Mr. A. J. Jolley, Mr. J. Upson, the Rev. , Neville Wilson, and the Chairman of the committee (the Rev. Canon Stevenson) be appointed to consider as to what steps should be taken to provide increased accommodation in connection with this school, and report to the committee thereon. Canon MORLEY STIMENSON explained that the steps above detailed were in every case the carrying out of recommendations which had been made by the Board of Education inspectors. He was told it was feared that possibly the visit of the ladies who had been invited to act as an advisory committee might be regarded as an act of interference. Nothing was further from the thoughts or intentions of the committee than that, it was strongly impressed upon them by the Government
lewa;

inspectors thateeing that there were a large number of girls and boys in the school ana that the head teacher was a man, it was very desirable that certain ladies should go in from time to time, take an interest in the children, confer with the women teachers,and especially interest themselves in such subjects as needlework and cookery. A strong representation was made by the inspectors as to the necessity of further increasing the school. That was a very serious ques- tion. It meant, in whatever way it might be done, additional expenVi. At the present time the school was quite full and they were imable to admit a great many children who wished for admission. So far, that was satisfactory, but it was a great question to con- sider what was the best and most economical way of making the extension. A sub-committee had been appointed to thrash it out and present a report. The Rev. Father Vilisos seconded the adoption of the minutes.
Mr. MIY asked if the duties of the Advisory Corn- mittee would be clearly defined so as to show that there was do intention to interfere with the discipline or management of the school. . . . .

Mr. PirAltsToN asked if it was intended that the teachers should take it in turn to supervise the children during the dinner hour. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH inquired if the Committee could not make additional use of the Grammar School as he took it that the school was similar to the Secondary school. He thought it would he preferable to accommo- date more pupils at the Grammar School than to increase the size of the Secondary school. Canon MORLEY STEVENSON said the duties of the ladies who would visit the Secondary school would be distinctly defined and he thought Mr. May might rest assured that they would not in any way interfere with the discipline or conduct of the school. He thought the teachers would have to under- take in turn the superyision of the scholars who stayed at the School for dinner,but the duty would not fall often to each individual teacher. With regard to the additional accommodation, he was sure the corn- mittee would bear Mr. Fairclough's suggestion in mind. They must, howeuer, remember that the great difference between the Grammar School and the Secondary School —a necessary and right difference—was the amount of the fee. The committee had to cater for the boys whose parents could not afford to pay the Grammar School fees and that was making the pressure on the Secondary Schoollmore marked.
The Minutes were confirmed. SITES AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.

The Architect for the erection of the " Beamont " Council school having advised the Sites and Buildings Committee that, owing to the nature of the land, the walls of the Infants' department should be carried down to the clay bed about:three feet deeper than was origin- ally intended, it was resolved that permission be given to the Architect to make this alteration in the speciflca- Lionel, the probable additional cost not to exceed .RBO. A letter was submitted from Messrs. Clare and Bldg- ray, with reference to certain items included in the specification for the" Beamout Council school, and the Law Clerk was requested to arrange, if possible,

with the architect and the contractor for the variation of the terms of the specification so that, where manu- facturers' names are specified in respect of materials to be used, the words "or of equal quality" should be added. _ .

The MAYort in moving the confirmation of the minutes explained that the Local Government Board had sanctioned the plans for the erection of the " Beamont " Council School. The Board had also reduced the time for the repayment of the loan from 50 to 30 years. The letter from Messrs. Clare and Ridgway had reterence to bricks. In the specification Greengate bricks Nv.ere stipulated. It had been decided to altcr the specification to red " bricks of a su;table quality " so that no one would be prevented from tendering. The stipulation of f.,1 reengate bricks was a slip on the part of the architect. Alderman SMETJEURST seconded.

Councillor WILKINsos : lan sorry to find we have already an extra of all on the" Bearnont " school. In purchasing land it would be better if we wont more deeply into the matter and asked the opinion of some- one who was born on the site—someone who could toll how many years he had skated upon it. The minutes were approved. I

Crappenball Woman's Sudden Death. Mr. Yates, district coroner, held an inquest at the Dog and Dart Inn, Grappenhall, on Monday, on the body of Mary Booth, (51), wife of Joseph Booth, cabinetmaker, Waste-lane, Thelwall, who died suddenly on Saturday evening.—Elizabeth Raymond,of G ra ppe n- hall, said she was standing at her door on Saturday night shortly after nine o'clock when she heard some- one say "Oh dear." She found that the deceased was lying on her face. With assistanca she got her into the house and undid her dress at the neck. She breathed once, closed her eyes, and died.—Evidence was given by the husband to the effect that the deceased had complained of her heart troubling her.—Dr. Jago said the probable cause of death was heart failure. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence.

div.head: Total 437 Total 323 Majority for St. George's, 114. UNKNOWN FACTS ABOUT CURRANTS.
div.p: Total 437 Total 323 Majority for St. George's, 114. UNKNOWN FACTS ABOUT CURRANTS.

If young mothers, and indeed all those whose duty it is to cater for a household, only knew what h cheap valuable food there is ready to hand in dried currants, the fruit would be/on the table every day. These little grape berries contain over three times as much actual nourishment as lean beef, and are-abundant in the right kind of sugar required to supply the body with energy and vitality. Currants contain several most important delicious fruit acids, which not only cool the blood and help the digestion, but prevent skin complaints. Currants eaten as dessert are as wholesome as they are palatable, and there are scores of ways of cooking them. For children currants are an ideal article of food. They are eaten with delight, and are, consequently, more profitable to the youngsters than food which is unpalatable. The action of the currant is gently and naturally laxative and its use is altogether conducive to good health.

COMMERCIAL FA I LlME'.—According to Kernp's Mercantile Gazette, the total number of Commercial Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, December 13th, was 169, viz. :—New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 92 ; Deeds of Arrangement registered, 77. Fhe respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 92 ; Deeds of Arrangement, 192—Total 181 ; being a decrease of 15. The total num- ber of Commercial Failures recorded during the 50 weeks of the present year is 8,687 ; the total number recorded in the corresponding 50 weeks of list year was ; 8,601, showing an increase of 86.

div.head: WATERWORKS QUESTION.
div.p: THE WATERWORKS QUESTION.
LIVELY DISCUSSION AT THE SPECIAL COUNCIL MEETING.
"MAYORAL INFALLIBILITY."

After nearly tvvol hours' discussion the Warrington Town Council at a special meeting on Friday evening rescinded the minute of the Water Committee confirmed on July 4th last, which read as follows :—" That the tender of Messrs. James Simpson and Son Ltd., of London, for compounding the beam engine at Winwick Pumping Station at £1,530 be accepted." Our readers will remember that application has already been made to the Local Government Board for permission to borrow the money for the compounding of the engine, but a strongly-worded and influentially-signed protest against the expenditure has been forwarded to that authority. The meeting was presided over by the Mayor (Alder- man Bolton) and there were also present : Aldermen Fairclough (deputy Mayor), Bennett, Evans, and Smethurst, Councillors Wilson, Evans, Skelland, Ashcroft, Lord, Barton, Wilkinson, Forshavr, Clegg, Hulse, Sankey, Peacock, Fulton Smith. Wright, Cliantler, Roberts, Dr. Joseph, Craik, Stott, Dickenson, Benson and Burton, and the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) and other officials. In an opening statement the MAvort, after reviewing the history of the matter, said it appeared to him to be a dangerous practice, and not unattended with groat risk, to attempt to undo the work of the Council six months after a resolution has been passed. He did not know, but it was quite possible, that Messrs. Simpson and Co. had rep red the plant for the compounding of , the engine. With reference to the observations which.had been made regarding the printing of notices of motion in the Council summons which were subsequently ruled out of order, he would call the attention of the Council to their Standing Order No. 2, which required the Town Clerk to insert in the summons for meetings of the Council, in addition to such matters as might be ordered by the Mayor, all notices of motion which might have been received by him five clear days before the day of the meeting. That was a matter in which the Town Clerk had no option, and it was not for him to decide whether the notices of motion were to be inserted in the Council summons or not. With regard to the claim made by a member at the last meeting to have the names of the voters recorded, no member had a right to make such demand, either under the Municipal Corporations Act or the Standing Orders of the Council. That was the law on the subject, and under which he intended to carry out the business of the Council. The meeting had not been in progress long when a lively passage at arms occurred. Councillor PENIBERTON, who formally moved the rescinding of the acceptance of the tender, questioned the ruling which the Mayor had given. The MAYOR (interrupting) : I don't want any dis- cussion at all. I have to conduct the business of the meeting on my own lines, according to the Standing Orders. as I interpret them. I want nothing but what is straight and above board. Every motion submitted to the Council has to be straightforward and above board, so that it cannot he misconstrued. You must speak to this motion, Councillor Pemberton, and you must let the thing drop. Councillor PEMBERTON : But you make a statement, Mr. Mayor, and it goes forth to the Press, and I should certainly have a chance of explaining. The MAYOR (warmly) : You are not coin., to dictate to me about the manner of conducting the business of the Council. Councillor PEIBERTON : lam not going to dictate to von. The MAyott : Then let the matter drop. Councillor PEMBERTON : I shall ask the Council to— __ __ .
The NrAYOR : Very well, then. You must call a Council meeting. Go on with the engine business,

- Councillor PEMBERTON : You have made a state- ment, Mr. Mayor, and I wish to explain that— The MAYOR: Are we to have the business meeting or not? (One or two voices: " Business meeting"). Councillor PEMBERTON : Only two members spoke. . . .
The M A VOR : You must stick'to the Council maion. • .

Councillor PEMBERTON: You have not done so. The MAYOR: I gave an explanation, and I have a right to do so. (Warmly and ringing the bell). Sit, down, and let us go on with the business. , Councillor PEMBERTON: I ask the Council to hear my explanation. Tne MAYOR: You go on with the business first. I am not going to be dictated to. Councillor PEMBERTON: It is most unfair to make a statement which you will not allow me to put right. It is a marvellous way of conducting the business of the Council and most un-English. Giving his reasons for moving the rescieding„ of the Council's previous decision, Councillor -Pemberton con- tended that it would ben waste of money to compound the engine, which was thirty-five years old, but he had no objection to £250 or £3OO being spent on repairs. Continuing, the Councillor said one thing he strongly resented—and he was sorry to have to say it—was this : it Was wrong that officials of the Corporation should speak to individual members on any position they took up. If they objected to something they did not think was right it was highly improper that they should go to to any individual member and ask " Why did you do that ?" There was no doubt that that had been done for a few years, and he asked the Council in an unmis- takable manner to stop them doing so. The motion was seconded by Councillor Lord who said that since the last Council meeting strong action had been taken. The Local Government Board had been Approached, and he had not the slightest doubt that the Board would not grant the loan. Ho had consulted two or three engineers in Warrington,and they said this job could be done for half the estimated cost, and that the engine could be put in thorough repair for £2OO or .£3OO. The compounding was ft very simple matter, and could be done for one half the cost. Why they should go .out of Lancashire, which was the home of beam engines and compounding, or why they should go out of Warrington he did not know. Alderman BENNETT said he was extremely sorry it had been necessary to have this meeting, and he could not help thinking that it could have been avoided. It was 'unfortunate that motions should be allowed to be put down if they were not in order, but when they were allowed to be put down and then refused lie thought they ought to have some explanation at the time. Again these two motions were the same now as before, and he could not see exactly how thel were out of order before and right now. The MAyon : You can do what you like at this meeting, but you were proceeding on the motion before. Continuing, he said they put him in the chair to do the chairman's work and he did it according to his reading of the rules. He gave his ruling and did not want to argue about it. They must accept it that he was prac- tically infallible in the position he occupied, and accept his ruling. Alderman i3ENNETT : [accept your ruling, but I don't accept your logic. (Laughter, rind hear, hear.) The iSayort I Take it for granted that lam infalli- ble. ( Laughter.) The matter was discussed at great length, Alderman Evans, who explained the matter from the Water Com- mittee's standp3int, contending that the compounding of the engine was the most economical scheme. The voting was as follows : FOR RESCINDING. COBB. James Evans. „ Barton. „ Skelland. „ Ashcroft. „ .Joseph. „ Roberts. „ Forshaw. • Chantler. „ Dickenson. If Lord. „ Benson. • Pemberton, „ Stott. Wright. „ Crai k. Hulse. „ Burton. —l7 THE LAWSON CONTRACT.
AGAINST. Aid. Fairclough. ~ Smethurst. . J. Evans. C'oun. Fulton Smith „ Peacock. L.-5
DID NOT VOTE. Aid. Bennett. Conn, Wilson. „ Sankey. Wilkinson. t. Clegg,

div.head: Branch Banks.
div.p: The Branch Banks.

A successful year's work was reviewed at the annual' meeting of the trustees and managers of the Warrington Srevinis Bank which was hold on Tuesday. Mr. W. Long- (chairman) presided and there were also present :—Mr. John Geddes (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. Yonge. W. Bracecamp, H. V. Pigot, .1. H. G. Hollingworth, Councillor Craik, Messrs. C. D. Parkinson, J. H. - Smethurst, Robson J. Chorley, J. S. Hill, J. Longland, C. Jackson Holmes, W. Richardson, W. Tinsley, G. Dakin, C. White, and W. 4. Proud (actuary). THE REPORT. The Committee of Management submitted to the- Trustees and Managers the 88th annual report. It stated that a brancn bank was opened at Earlestown on the 16t11 January last and had made steady progress. For the benefit and convenience of the residents in the west of the Borough, premises had been secured in Green-street, Bank Quay, and it was intended to open a branch there at an early date. After carefully con- sidering the Savings Bank Act, 1904, the committee had decided to open a Special Investment Department, thus giving to the depositors extra facilities for saving and also adding to the usefulness of the Institution. The following was a summary of the transactions during the year and included the business of the branch Bank : 910 accounts had been opened or renewed and 413. closed, leaving 14,429 open accounts ; an increase of 492' on the year. There have been 20,245 deposits, and 9,997 pavments,maki n g together 30,242 transactions, an increase in .deposits of 1,320, and a decrease in payments of 285. The amount now due to depositors was £352,431 18s. 10d and the amount of Stock held by depositors was £17,852 Os. 2d., making a total of £370,283 19s. The assets of the Bank were as follows, vii. :—invested with commis- sioners on General Account, £350,807 Gs. 4d. ; invested with commissioners on Surplus Fund Accounts, £4,500 ; I Government 5t0ck,£17,852 Os 3d ; balance in Treasurer's Hands, 3,016 2s. 9d. ; Freehold Premises and Furniture, £1,300 : total £377,475 9s. 3d. • leaving a surplus after paying depositors in full of .C 7,191 10s. 3d. The net profit, after Paying all current expenses and the cost of furnishing the Earlestown Branch, was £2IG 19s. 10d. In addition to the Stock held for Depositors £17,852 hs. 2d., the National Debt Commissioners had in their hands £355, 307 Gs. 4d., which was considerably in excess of the total liabilities. The Committee regretted having to record the deaths of Mr. Henry Milling, a Trustee, of the Reverend Richard Greenall and Mr., Thomas Birchall, Managers and members of the Manage- ment Committee.

THE BRANCH BANKS. The CHAIRMAN', in formally moving the adoption of the accounts, which were submitted along with the above statement, alluded to the opening of the branch Bank at Earlestown. He said the Committee of Management had felt for some time that they would like to move in that direction as they believed it would be a -great encouragement of thrift among the people to take their banks, as far as possible, to the doors of the depositors, especially in neighbourhoods where large works were situated. The Earlestown branch would hive lzeen open .for twelve-months on 7finuary IGth cud he thought he might say it had been a success. They were about to open another branch bank at Bank Quay, where there were several large works,and they hoped it would be even more useful than the one at Earlestown. The reoentls -opened special investment department seemed to be a very good move indeed. Although the fund was only established on November 21st there was close upon £6.000 invested in it. Mr. Long quoted from the report of the Hull Bank showing that the sum invested in the special investment depart- ment there was £760,722. He had great hopes of the success of the new department at Warrington. (Hear hear). It had been founded for the benefit of those depositors who had paid into their account in the bank the full amount allowed by the Act of Parliament (Z 200 and were therefore compelled to seek investments else- where. The whole of the report tended to show that the bank was steadily growing. They must be doing some good to their poorer neighbours by enabling them to make provision for a rainy day. Mr. Long. con- cluded by expressing regret that during the sear they had suffered the loss of two valuable members of the Managing Committee—Mr. Thos. Birchen and the Rev. Richard Greenall. Mr. GiEDDEs seconded and the motion was carried. The Rev. H. V. PIGOT moved that the repqrt of the committee of management be approved, and that the meetinc acknowledge the services rebdered to the institution by the gentlemen acting on the committee. The work, he said, had been a labour of love to most of the members. They had served diligently, faithfully and punctually for many years in a work which to many would be dry and uninteresting and had made the- institution a very valuable one to the working classes. Mr. C. D. PARKINSON seconded and congratulated the committee on their progressive attitude which, he thought, would make the bank of even greater benefit. The motion was heartily agreed to. E LF.CTION S. Mr. C. WHITE moved that Mr. W. Long and Mr. J. Geddes be re-elected chairman and vice-chairman respectively. He did not think they could fled two genlemen who took more interest in the institution or who were better qualified to occupy the positions. The Rev. Jottx YONGE seconded and the motion was carried.
WOUI I-Arm:try fa

Mr. LONG and Mr. GEODES briefly returned thanks. Mr. JACKSON HOLMES proposed, and Mr.RICHARDSON seconded, ti at the Rev. John Yonge and Mr. T. B. Cuter be elected to the Board of Management. The Rev. JOHN YONOE thought it would be a good thing if some new blood were introduced. There had been two or three deaths but there did not seem to be any suggestion of filling up the vacancies. He proposed the appointment of Mr. Josiah Longland. It was agreed that the three gentlemen named should be added to the Committee.

The following were appointed additional managers The Revs. J.lCarnson, C. Harvey Cook, J. R. J011(1?, G. Vale Owen, W. Pollock-Hill and A. F. White, and Messrs. John Taylor, J. B. Isaac, C. E. Parker, J. G. Withinshaw, Henry Milling, W. Monks, Vera B. Davies, R. Dobson, G. F. F. White, W. EL Stansfield, J. W. Parker. A. Cornev, T. D. Amos, C. Turner, G. W. A. Brown, T. J. Lee, Dr. Watkins, Dr. Valentine, and Mr. %V. Roberts.
SURETIES. On the motion of Mr. DAKIN, seconded by Mr. SMETIEuRsT, the list of securities by the officials was. approved.
THE STAFF THANKED.

Mr. LONG proposed a cordial vote of thanks to the staff of the Bank. He was sure that from the Actuary. downwards all did their work well. The vote was accorded. Mr. PROUD responded and said he was sure the staff' would highly appreciate the compliment.

div.head: HOW TO ESCAPE A "BLACK BOXING-DAY."
div.p: HOW TO ESCAPE A "BLACK BOXING-DAY."

The stomach being an organ of delicate human tissue, and not a " cast-iron arrangement," rebels against the of heavy feeding and the irregularities of tho holiday season. Sick headaches, dizziness, specks before- the eyes, coated tongues, bilious attacks, insomnia, palpitation, nod vomiting are the penalties of rich and poor alike. The best cure is bile beans, because they give the liver and stomach just that natural assistance• which these organs need to-day, without the griping or purging following doses of old-fashioned remedies. Bile beans are composed of certain valuable herbal extracts,. which have the power of doing tired Nature's work. They strengthen the digestive organs, create a healthy' appetite,remove all discomfort after feeding. and, more- over make the rich food we take do us good instead of' harm.

With such indoor frivolities and mlldnesses the She looked further, to find out with whom he days passed enjoyably—for the house party at was quarrelling. Comte La Motte, without his well-trimmed Frey

be,arct was talking quietly in plain English, from which all foreign accent had been expunged. "It is no use to make a disturbance," he waa !laying. "I recognised you at once. Since you have passed three times through my hands I could not do otherwise. It was a Clever dodge, but it has failed, and you must pay the penalty. Here, officer." While handcuffs were being fastened on, the spurious Comte turned and saw Delia. "Pardon me, Miss Somerville," he said, in the courteous tone he had used at dinner, "hut this is no scene for you. lam sorry to say the gen- tleman who has been welcomed in your house as a guest is no other than a common thief—the missing jewellery has been found among his effects, ready to be carried off to-morrow. While you were dancing "—and the detective laughed as lie uttered the word—" his luggage was being ransacked." Without movement or cry she stood listening to all that was said. Dainty Delia the inamorata of a common felon! This terrible revelation came slowly to her. When it had fully dawned, then, and not till then, did she cry out in a spasm of agony, and, tottering on her feet, she fell backwards into the arms oi the watchful Lorimer, who would have given his life to have kept this evil from her, and who felt he could never forgive himself for having been instrumental in bringing this man into her life. He carried her away, and laid her on the sofa in her little boudoir, dainty as herself with its many beauteous attributes. There, with her mother, he left her, and walked slowly away, such a look of regret and of deep love on his expressive. if unhandsome, face as is seldom seen but once in a lifetime. Before Delia recovered consciousness the fuss was over; the supposed Comte La Motte and his prisoner were gone, accompanied by the officer in plain clothes who had been playing at valet in the servants' quarters, till his services were required. It was an episode brief in time, but lasting in recollection. Dainty Delia was cured for aye of reckless flirting, and though she did not at once respond to Harry Lorimer's ardent and devoted wooing, she had learnt the lesson which taught her to prefer real sterling gold to mere alloy; yet she felt too much ashamed to COWn all she felt, so crushed and humble was the by the descent from her pinnacle of daintiness, which she by her own folly had brought about. With patience Harry Lorimer waited through the long summer days, going everywhere in London where he was likely to meet Delia, bet making but little way. She remained coy and shy. When she thought of Bowring in a prison, all her heart turned cold—not because she still loved him, but because she scarcely thought she had the right to transfer a love that had once been his to this staunch and loyal Lorimer. At last, when autumn came, and they were once more thrown together in the comparative solitude of Craigie Castle, he deemed the time had come to give up mute devotion and urge his suit in passionate words. Delia could no longer resist. She sank into the arms that had borne her fainting to her room on that never to be forgotten night, and looking up into his face, smiled the promise her lips—once so pelt and saucy—were now too shy to utter. Ere Christmas came again Harry Lorimer claimed his bride, and with the forethought of a kindly man, bore her off to southern climes, where all recollection of that tempestuous snow-bound week should be obliterated in the dazzling sup slate of the prosont cloudiesa, Lappy hours.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.
TROUBLE ABOUT A MOTOR CAR EXCHANGE.

At the Birmingham Assizes on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Mucknill, Frederick Westwood and Gertrude Westwood, his wife, 50, Alcester-road, Moseley, brought an action against Herbert Plumpton, toolmaker, of 171, Liverpool-road, Warrington, for damages for wrr ugutri , conversion.—Mr. Hum Young nnd Mr. Heist (instructed by Messrs. Perry, Son, and Richards) appeared for plaintiffs, and Mr. Stanger, K.C., and Mr. Gandy (instructed by Messrs. Arthur Browne and Co., Warrington) for defendant. During the year, said counsel, the plaintiffs advertised that a 16 h.p. motor , car was wanted, the teams being exchange or cash. They received a reply from the defendant. Mr. Plump- ton wrote that he had a reliable car which plaintiffs might have examined by an expert. Plaintiffs wrote hack that in exchange for the car, with .£lO, they wotild give a pony and trap, a diamond ring, a diamond stud, rnd a care of cutlery. The plaintiffs went over to War- rington to examine the vehicle, but the defendant then , told them that it was not available for driving. At a later date defendant visited Moseley to inspect the ring and stud. Ho was permitted by Mrs. Westwood to take the jewellery awav on the understanding that he was to lime a valuation 'hy an expert, after which the articles were to be returned pending the completion of the negotiation. A receipt for the jewellery and ring was given. WeStwood, accompanied by an expert, then went over to Warrington. The car was examined by the expert, and Mr. Westwood was supplied with a report, which was not of A satisfactory character. He expressed the opinion that the car had not been driven a long distance. Mr. NVestwood communicated with the defendant, stating that in view of the report he would not have the car, and be asked for the return of the jewellery. The defendant replied that his view of

Ithe negotiations 'was that so far as th plaintiffs were Iconcerned they bad previously completed the bargain subject to an option on his part. He practically in- sisted said Mr. Young, upon the clenching of tke bar- gain. Plaintiffs then had no other remedy but to take proceedings. The plaintiffs having given evidence, the motor expert was called, who described the car from a trade point of view as a t freak." It had originally been well built,but it was old-fashioned and faulty. The I defence was that defendant was justified in his action, icontending that subiect to a certain option the bargain had been comp,ered by the plaint i ffs. lie stated that , they visited Warrington, and desired to take the car I with them. The only reason he refused was that they I had not brought with them the pony and trap. Mr. i Westwood stated that he was unable to do so because be had not given suilicient notice to the re iltfay company. He said that both the plaintiffs expressed themselves highly delighted with the car. He still adhered to the warrantry, urging that it was thoroughly sound. It was not modern, but that was never contended. The jewellery was lent to him to be tested, and he bad given a receipt for it. Defendant had not completed his evidence ‘Oren the Court adjourned. . At the resumed hearing of the case on Monday, the defendant conclnded his evidence, and after council , had addressed the Court on behalf of their respective clients, the jury returned a verdict in favour of the ' plain:iffs and judgment was entered accordingly.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES.
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES.
Last of the Series.

Tho last of the series of University Extension lectures on" A Trio of English essayists" was delivered in the, Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Friday evening by the Rev. %V. Lawrence Schroeder, M.A.. the subject being "The life and work of Thomas de Quincey." The lecturer said that of the greater characters of English literature few were so difficult to appraise as De Quincey. His personality, genius and style with all their unmistakable characteristics were drenched in mystery. The indubitable power of his genius both attracted and repelled. We were alternately fascinated and irritated by his style and at the end we knew not whether to enshrine him in our he.aits or to set him on the pedestal of a mute, admiring homage. Most of all men he exemplified the eccentricities of genius and sometimes we sighed for a little more commonseuse, a little less pendular), and bewildering superiority and a greater apprehension of the mind of the ordinary reader. Yet he (the lecturer) thought we should all proclaim our own sad lack if we pronounced De Quinces other than a mighty master of English prose. , The lecturer then gave an interesting review of the life of be Quincey, pointing out that one of the best ' features was the beautiful memory be ever had. of the poor outcast, Ann. It often made him (the lecturer) , feel that we might he shunning angels unawares when we gathered our cloaks together and passed some poor creatures in the streets. Speaking generally, De Quincey's life was a solitary one. His habits were strange and his methods of work bewildering, but be was faithful inn great measure to his intellectual ideals and did not neglect to cultivate the talents he possessed. He cars conscious of his learning and literary power but in all his curious boastiug there was truth. His intellect was of a remarkable order—keenly analytic. yet broadly comprehensive. In his writings ciassicisrns and colloquial slang jostled each other. His thought was usually clear and exactly expressed. Granted, the intellectual equipment, any reader could follow the development of his positions. Of simple pathos there was very little in his writing. When handling the pathetic,he preferred to move in stately solemn fashion. his humour was irony and one's appreciation of it de- pended on the subject and the application. One might summarise the quality of his style in a phrase :"Strong sublimity." His genius was more of the creative than of the critical order. His discursiveness made one sometimes blaspheme. The one thing which more than any other would hinder his vogue was lack of moral force. Tho distinguishing feature of his genius lay in its mystic quality. Alderman Tli.rssr.rr moved a vote of thanks to the lecturer and said the study of the great essayists in this age was one of the most necessary in which we could indulge. The Rev. C. HARVEY COOK seconded and the vote was heartily accorded.

At Saddieworth, on Wednesday, George Taylor was fined 10s. and costs for not having had proper control of a pony and trap. While he was in a public-house at Denshaw the pony bolted, and killed a buy who was playing in the road.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
DSCRIABGR 23rd 1905.
We wish all our readers a Happy Xmas and Bright New Year.
Our political oppon-

ents opened their election campaign on Tuesday with a Parr Hall meeting addressed by Earl Percy, M.P., a member of the late dis- credited administration. The meeting cannot by any stretch of imagination be said to augur well for the Tory cause, for it was neither crowded nor unanimous in feeling, and in neither respect cook; it he compared at all favourably with the Lloyd- George and Outhwaite meetings held by the Liberals during the slack season. If the enthusiasm of the Csnservatives saunot be worked up so near the election as we are now, then it may reasonably be presumed to be non-existent. The meeting on Tuesday was chiefly remarkable for the assiduity with which the speakers drew herrings across the political trail. It seemed to he their mission to c nfuse the real and pressing issues rather than to justify the faith that is in them and present a clear understandable case to the electorate. "No Home Rule " is plainly to be the rallying cry of the Tories at the election next month, and while not expressing it, they must possess a devout thank-- fulness that Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and Lord Rosebery have found them a peg on which to hang the cloak designed to cover all the misdeeds of the late Government. Men like the Premier, Mr. John Morley and Mr. Aspith are as staunch Home Rulers as ever they were ha the days of Mr. Gladstone's administration, and all Liberals admire their sincerity on the question. But it is not Home Rule that the nation is immediately concerned with, and all the efforts of ingenious Tory orators will not succeed in leading the electors up this blind alley. The people are concerned primarily and almost entirely with the attack on our fiscal policy and the introduction of Chinese slavery in S mth Africa. Earl Percy and his friends had nothing to say with regard to the inexplicable confusion which the divided opinions of Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. B ilfeur have thrown the country into. They did not avow themselves followers of either leader but endeavoured to formulate proposals which might accord with the irreducible minimum of one and the maximum of the other, but they were net concrete proposals. Earl Percy advocates a mild form of retaliation which would give power to " negotiate." So far as we can learn, the power to negotiate has never been lost in any trade where methods are np-to- date and business like. Mr. C lamberlain's "dying industries " are flourishing with the utmost con- tumacy from the Tiritf R•sformer's point of view, and the B iard of Trade returns show an ever- increasing national prosperity. To place poverty and unemployment at the fiscal door is simply to bag the question. Toose very serious problems require internal treatment and much is to be hoped from men like Mr. John Burns and his democratic colleag ies in regard to their ultimate solution. When Mr. Chamberlain stormed the country with a purely Protectionist plea and boldly advocated a 2i. tax on corn and the imposition of wholesale hostile tariffs he was dubbed a" whole-hogger." The very daring 'of his proposals earned him a transient ppularity. ,On the summit of that wave of feeling came Mr.„ R. Pierpoint M.P. He also was a" whole-hogger " as he explicitly avowed. To-day the wave has subsided and the flowing tide has sot in against Protection and all its attendant evils. BUt we are not going to forget that Mr. Piero frint is a -" whole-hogger " still. however he may modify his views to snit the peels of the occasion. Oa Tiles- day one might almost have thonght he was a Free Trader with no more harmful ideas than a preferential tariff to " bind the Colonies to our- selves for ever." We know already that even this little imperialistic dream is nothing but a dream. 'The Colonies will take all the preference they can .get from us, but they are not going to build a wall against foreign trade merely to foster Imperial union. Oh no! And we shall be surprised if the 'Warrington electors forget the day when Mr. Plerpoint proved himself a political opportunist, and swallow his new-found sophistries!
RED HERRINGS.
• The important appeal case TliE Sim CANAL affecting the dredging of ACTION. the Mersey at Warrington _ _

, by the Manchester Ship Canal Company has resulted in a cornplEte victory for the Warrington traders. The Canal Company, it will bs remembered; appealed against the late Mr. Justice Byrne's decision which enforced their statutory obligations to dredge the bed and the banks of the river. After an exhaustive hearing the Court of Appeal on Thursday decided against the company and the appeal was dismissed with costs. The company wal therefore have to maintain a depth of water of eight feet so as to allow for the navigation of ships which require that amount of water. The judgment is an important one for Warrington 4s it should permanently secure the commercial advantages accruing from a full use of the waterway. Of course, the Canal Company have still the alternative of appealing to the House of Lords, but we should imagine it ilhighly improbable that they will adopt this course, especially in view of , the fact that all three judges who heard the I appeal concurred in the decision.
The Winwick beam No COMPOUNDING. engine is on its "beam

_ . ends" so far as the compounding sclierne is concerned. At the special meeting last Friday Councillor Pemberton carried his motion to rescind the contract for compounding the engine at £1,530 by 17 votes to 5 aftor a lengthy discussion. The case for the scheme was made to appear very weak by its critics, and there was ample proof that, in the first place, the engine was only required as a stand-by, and secondly that compounding would not increase its capacity for pumping water by a single gallon. There was nothing to rebut the contention that the expendi- ture of £2OO to .000 would put the engine in almost as good condition as ever, find at least make it quite efficient for the work it was called upon to do. The watch-dogs of the Council have gained a signal triumph in regard to this matter and they are to be congratulated on having prevented the unnecessary expenditure of at least £l,OOO of public money.

Prior to the Council meet- TOWN COUNCIL ing the Mayor drew attention PROCEDUILIS. to " observations which have been made regarding the printing of notices of motion in the Council Summons which are subsequently ruled out of order" and quoted the Standing Orders to show that the Town Clerk was obliged to insert all such notices which have been received by him n in the specified time. If this is the ruling then another amendment cif the Standing Orders is urgently required. As matters stand at present the atten- dance of aldermen and councillors to discuss the business of the agenda is nothing more or less than a farce. It has frequently happened of late that the most important and contentious items have been contained in notices of motion, and the members of the Council have come prepared with fact and ideas for use in debate on these motions only to be told at the last minute that the matter is - "out of order," and as happened in the most recent instance without any explanation as to why or wherefore. This is anything but businesslike, and no wonder msriy of the members of the council- are resentful at the waste of time and effort which has been involved by such procedure. It seems to us that an amend- ment of the Standing Orders is required on the following lines: All notices oF motion should he immediately revised by the Town Clerk or Ws Deputy and if out of order the proposer should be at once informed in order that he may make his motion in conformity .with all requirements. For all motions to go to the council whether in order or not is a sheer absurdity and we can only wonder that it has been tolerated so long by a body of business men whose special duty it is to administer the town's affairs.

Th e Warrington A YEsa's THRIFT. Savings Bank is pre- eminently a working class institution, and its continued prosperity which is always, happily,revealed with the approach of Christmas is cause for real gratification. To people who realize the wisdom of providing for the well nigh inevitable "rainy day" and who are only able to accumulate their savings by small instalments the bank is a great boon. That it is' appreciated is evident from the fact that during the year there has been an increase in the number of accounts of 492 and in deposits of 1,320. From the financial standpoint the state of affairs is emin,ntly satisfactory. After paying depos;tors in full there wou'd be a surplus of £7,191 103. 3d., and the net profit on the year's working amounted to £216 19. 10d. The opening of a branch bank at Earlestown has proved to he a wise step and we are glad to hear that at an early 4ate another branch will be established for the convenience of residents in the Bank Quay neigh- bourhood. It is certainly an additional encourage. merit to thrift when the banks are, as the chair man aptly put it, brought to the doors of deposi- tors and the progresreve attitude of the committee is to be commended.

Shall the date of WALKING Day. our greatest local festival.-- Walking Day—be altered? The question has once more been brought to the fore, mainly at the instiga- tion of the tradesmen of the town, hut on Mon- day the Education Committee—which would of course exercise considerable influence by taking a decided attitude—declined to commit itself in Favour of a change to the Friday before August Bank Holiday. So many interests are invoivel that an alteration cannot be agreed to without van, careful consideration. Tradesmen coin plait no doubt with perfect justification—of the disloa- tion of business, and consequent loss, occasioned by this purely local holiday which intervenes between Whitsuntide and August. But thern is also the point of view of the manufacturer. Several large firms, it was painted out, arrange for their annual stock-taking to be made durin,, Walking Diy week an in that case it is fitting that the festiv d should be held when many workmen are compul- sorily idle. Sentiment also enters into the stitject, to some extent and there are people who wood not readily consent to the merging of the " children's day "into an ordinary bank holiday. It is. we understand, probable that a town's meeting will he called, and then we shall have the c Liu dci ttad from all standpoints.

"0.-B." is almost semi-Acial now ; and if " Joe " is not likely to become that, it Will at least hold its place securely with "Pam," " Dizzy," and " Labby " in familiar, purely human talk.—" Pall Mill Gazette." * * * _ _

Though the last Parliam—entary session was barren in its actual results there were no fewer than 364 divisions. We notice that Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., voted 207 times. We shall have more to say as to the way he voted later. * * * . _

Mr. Michael Davitt has la-aen writing to the " Daily News" to compliment that journal on its exposure of the whole-hog and hall-hog pretence ofMessrs.Chambei-- lain and, Balfour, respectively, to. fight an anti-Free Trade combat under the guise of an anti-Irish crusade.

* The weather prospects for Christmas are very fair; mild weather and a " green Christmas "seem as near certain as anything in the way of atmospheric prediction can be. An expert considers that the weather is likely to become cooler, with a slight tendency to fog. Any- thing almost but the latter !

*** In the course of a warm discussion as to order of procedure at tim Council meeting on Friday last, the Mayor laid down the dictum that in his official capacity he was practically infallible. The Council laughed, and Alderman Bennett replied pertinently to his Worship : I accept your ruling, but I don't accept your logic. * *

Councillor Evans and -Mr. Upson had a warm but friendly passage at arms at the meeting of the Educa- tion Committee on Monday. Both speakers declared their intention of " hitting and hitting hard" hut Alderman Sinetbuist's original suggestion that " bax- ing gloves should be brought in" met with a gentle remonstrance from the chair. 5*5 . _

, - The re-print by us of Mr. It. L. Outhwaite's War- rington speech, which was issued in pamphlet form by the Liberal Association, has resulted in a unique demand for copies from all parts of the country. This week the Association has dispatched a parcel to Mr. Seddon, the labour candidate for Newton Division, to help in his fight with Colonel Pilkington, M.P. * * Mr. Henry Vivian, who was on Wednesday finally ' adopted by the Birkenhead Liberals as their candidate in the forthcoming Parliamentary election, ' said that one section of their opponents were appealing to every- thing that was lowest in human nature. He hoped that no Liberal -would attempt to compete with such methods, for he would rather lose the contest than lose his self-respect.

* * Owing to the resignation of the. Conservative Government and the consequent change in the office of the Attorney-Genmal, some delay must necessarily ensue in obtaining a reply to the application of the Town Council for leave to proceed against two mem- bers for alleged breach of the Corrupt Practices Act. The Town Clerk reported to the General Purposes Committee to this effect on Monday. * *

The police in Hanley ha-ve no trouble with pace- devouring motorists, and the latter have no fear of over-officious constables. The reason is to be found on, or in, the roads. The Hanley Chief Constable told the Watch Committee on Tuesday that they had not had a sir4,Yle motor-car case, and he could not imagine them having one. The roads were such that the vibration would smash the cars to pieces.

* * * Mr. A. H. Crosfielcl telegraphed to Mr. Lloyd-George last week end on behalf of the Liberal Association and Progressive Labour League, congratulating him upon his appointment to office in the new Government He has had the followino•° reply : —"December 15th, Wandsworth Common. Crostield, Hoylake.—Many thanks Warrington Liberals for congratulations. Every success to you in coming contest. Lloyd George." * * *

As was expected, the new Government reverts to tile new rule laid down by Mr. Gladstone and Lord Rosebery, but departed from by Mr. Balfour, requir- ing its members to surrender directorships of public companies. One or two minor offices, it is believed, were refused by those to whom they were offered on this account, but the Government apparently has lost no essential membn through the Prime Minister's insistence on all being like " Cesar's wife above suspicion.' * * Speaking at the Warrington Conservative Club on Wednesday, Colonel Pilkington, M.P., said " The foreign record of the late Government was the finest of any English Government during the whole of the last century. We had made friends with America, France, Spain, and Japan, and had also settled the trouble in Egpyt." He, of course, made no allusion to the big South African blot on the record which represents the loss of 25,000 British lives, £250,000,000 and the introduction of Chinese slavery under the flag. *s* There was an amusing instance of " rapid conver- sion "at the Education Committee's meeting on Mon- day. Mr. T. May seconded and spoke in support of a recommendation that the date of Walking Day should be altered. The persuasive eloquence of the opponents of the change must have carried greater weight than his own reasonings for when a vote was taken, Mr. May was seen to oppose the scheme which he had a short time before commended to the acceptance of the meeting. Mr. May can take credit to himself on reflecting that, as the time-honoured adage quoted by Councillor Evans says, "wise men chaage their minds, but fools never." * * It is not often that one sees a cow surveying the contents of a sweet shop from a position of vantage behind the counter, but such a spectacle was presented on Monday. Leaving the Norton Arms yard the animal calmly walked into an adjoining shop and entered into possession, the lady in charge beatine• hasty retreat. Passers-by were astonished to seec.the cow contemplating the dainties displayed in the window. Excitement ran high while several ventur- ous youths were engage ti in removing the contents of the shop and it was not until the counter had been displaced that the unwelcome intruder could be ejected.

Hands off ! We have no doubt whatever that all right-thinking and fair-minded voters in Warrington will resent with all an Englishman's love of fair play, the cowardly and vulgar attacks of Mr. J. J. Hands on Miss Crestichl. - This misguided individual seems to he taking every opportunity of misrepresenting Miss Crosileld's henest and outspoken criticism into an attack on the workiingman and his children. Whatever Miss Crosfield said on a subject entirely apart from politics has nothing whatever to do with her brother's candi- dature, and it is playing the game very low down to make a lady the butt of ill-bred sneers on the public platform. We hope in common decency that the Conservative leaders will repudiate Mr. Hands and his offensive peurilities. If not,the public has its own way of showing contempt for such electioneering methods.

* * Earl Percy is rapidly becoming tarred with the Chamberlain brush.—Exaggeration, half-truths and a wonderfully deceptive imagination. Every vote given to the present Government, &c., &.?.. What has : Earl Percy done? We do not hesitate to say that out of the gathering assembled at the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening-last not more than a quarter knew that there was such an individual. The fact that lie : was a real, live Earl attracted many to go and see whether he was in any way different from an ordinary man. We have often beard of Earls and " sich ' being stalwartyn the side of Protection so that we were not surprised to find that he was a kind of follower of " the orchid," but not a" whole hogger " like the present Member for Warrington, Mr. Robert Pierpoint. * Earl Percy said on Tuesday " They could dismiss the idea that Whites could do the unskilled work in the mines if allowed." Could they ? Not if they want to know the truth. In the Village Reef Mine, of which Mr. Creswell wis manager, in spite of the fact that White wages were Os. or 10s. a day, white labour was as economical in certain departments of unskilled work as coloured indentured labour at Is. Gd. :The fact of the matter is that White men can do the work, but, for other reasons, they are being kept out of it. Earl Percy should stick to faets. There would be plenty of " unskilled "labour in the mines if it were not for one reason alone—a British subject is , entitled to a vote and a Chinaman in a compound is not.

GARLAND, 51 to 55, bridge st., Warring- too.—Advt. Death of Miss Braide.

We record with regret the death, which took place on Wednesday, of Miss Margaret Elizabeth Braide (36), only surviving daughter of Mr. Edward Braide, the Clee, Walton New-road, Walton, late district goods manager to the London and North-Western Railway Company. Deceased had been in a failing state of health for some time and recently underwent an operation, from the effects of which she never recovered. She was actively associated with St. Paul's Church and her death will be regretted by a large circle of friends. The funeral will take place to-ay (Saturday) at the Warrington Cemetery.
PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

Warrington Catholic Young Men's Society. On Thursday evening the Rt. Rev. Abbot Smith, of Ampleforth, paid a visit to the rooms of the Society on his way home from Rome, The Rt. Rev. Abbot during a private audience which he had with His Holiness the Pope, obtained a special Apostolic bless- ing for the members of the Society, and the Pope wrote a special message to them with his own hand on a large portrait of himself, which the Rt. Rev. Abbot ISmith brought with him, and presented to the Society. The Rt. Rev. Father Abbot addressed the members, and gave a short interesting account of his audience with the Pope, and then bestowed on them the Apostolic Benediction.—Mr. 0. Toole (president C.Y.11.5.) occupied. the chair, and was supported by Father Swarbreck, 0.5.8., (chaplain C.Y.11.5.), Fathers I Whittle, Baines. and Buggins, and there was a large attendance of members.
Galvanized Booting Sheets, Roofing Felts, eze. Large stock.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Meeting of the Distress Committee. . _

The p—rincipal business at the meeting of the War- rington Distress Committee which was held on Tues- day, was the considering of applications for the post of clerk and enquiry officer to the Labour Enquiry Sub-Committee. Twenty-five applications were received, and five candidates were invited to attend a meeting of the Committee which will be held to-night (Friday.) The Deputy Town Clerk reported the receipt from the Local Government Board of a regulation with regard to the granting of relief to persons who have during the 12 months previous to the 10th October been relieved by means of the poor rate. The order made it possible for the Committee, having satisfied themselves that the applicant was a fit person to he relieved, to request the Local G wernmen Board to authorise them to entertain the application H. M. Astrrox's LIFE Tomo takes away that tired feeling.—(Advt.)
