Christmas Pantomime.

Patrons of the Royal Court Theatre are promised , a great attraction for the Christmas holidays in the shape of a new pantomime production " Mother Goose." The story is based on the time honoured fairy tale ani is full of humorous incidents and situations and will be presented by a strong com- pany. Among the artistes will be included a number of well-known musical comedy stars most of whom are already favourites in!:Warrington and the pro- duction promises to be a highly successful and enjoy- able one.

CHRISTAIAS PRESENTS.—Dressing-Caseq, Umbrellas and Gloves.—J. E. WHITE, 22, Sankey St.—Advt. Organ Recital. At the monthly recital. at St. Paul's Church on Sunday a short programme was played by Mr. E, Wilkes, the organist. The pieces incliided the "Slumber Song," and the intermezzo from "Cavalleria Rusticana." The vocalist was Mr. Levi Richardson, who contributed the recit and aria " Comfort ye " and !` Every Valley" from the " Messiah," his ren- dition of these difficult numbers from Handel's great work being much enjoyed. The recitals are highly appreciated and on Sunday evening there was a large congregation.

PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER TIIE CLOCK Foil BEST BOOTS IN L ANC ASH IRE.—Advt. Drowned In a Clay Pit. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at War- rington on Monday, on the body of William Reid, aged two years and five months (son of Robert Reid, wire cleaner, 213, Knutsford-road), who was found drowned in the clay pits at Latchford on Saturday afternoon. Thomas Connor, fitter, 15, Brook-street, said that at 'half-past three on S3turday afternoon he was playing football in a field off Knutsford-road. He beard that a child was in a clay pit and at once proceeded there. With the •assistance of others, the body was got out and artificial respiration rf as tried. Dr, Braide was sent for, and on arrival he said the child was dead. In answer to the Coroner, witness stated that the field was an open one, and was abont 50 yards away from the road, where people were allowed to walk. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," there being no evidence to show how the child got into the water. School Attendance Officers Meeting.

The annual meeting of the Scho TE Attendance Officers' Association was held on Saturday in the Education Office, Sankey-street, Warrington. Mr. Martindale of Earlestown occupied the chair. There were also present : —Messrs. P. E. Clough, William limber, Win. Rutter, T. F. Hughes,' J. Todd, and Wm. Farrar. The Secretary's report was read and confirmed. The Tieasurer brought forward his balance sheet, which was pissed. The following officials were appointed for the ensuing year : President, Mr. Thos. Martindale of Earlestown ; vice- mesident, Mr. Thos. Dromilow of St. Helens ; secre- tary and treasurer, Mr. Wm. Farrar of Warrington;. committee, Messrs. }limber ; Mercer, Pasquill, Rutter, and Clough. A hearty vote of thanks was accuded to the retiring officers. Mr. J. Todd, was enrolled as a member of the Association. ASK for CINNLNGHAit'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt.

Warrington and District Teachers' Association A general meeting of the members of the above was held on Saturday last at the Wycliffe Memorial Hall, Mr. S. Jeffery presiding over a fair attendance. Mrs. Stansfield was appointed secretary of the Ladies' Bureau. With reference to the nominations for the Executive of the National Union of teachers it was decided to support the candidature of Mr. Pickles, of Burnley, for the presidency,Mr. Hamilton as treasurer, and Messrs. Pickles and Pearson as members of the Executive representing Lancashire. The conference of teachers will beheld at Scarborough in Easter week and Messrs. W. H. Stapsfield, J. Upson, J. Wright, J. Cann, S. W. Jeffery, Wilcox, Mrs. Stansfield and Miss Brooks were appointed to represent the local associa- tion. Some discussion ensued on Superannuation Reform and the proposals of the Executive were approved. A committee, having for its objects the encouragement of sports sud games amongst school children under the supervision of the teachers, was chosen as follows :—Messrs. Morgan, Bowen,Goulden, Malcolm, G. J. Brown and the Misses M. Taylor and G. Jewkes.
J. E. Minn, 22, Sankey Street for Silk Nlafflars and Ties for XMAS PrtESENTS.—Advt. Popular Penny Concert. - - -

• Another large audience assembled at the popular penny concert held in Bold-street schools on Saturday evening. The programme was an exceptionally attrac- tive one, having been arranged by Mr, James Dodds, and was given almost entirely by well-known Liver- pool artistes. All acquitted themselves admirably and encores were the order of the evening, Miss Maudstry gave very expressive renderings of Scenes that are brightest," and " Waiting" and Mr, G. Platt inter preted "Land of hops and glory " and " The yeoman's wedding" with fine spirit. Mr. T. Canavan was heard to distinct advantage in "The star of Bethlehem." One of the most amusing features was a comic interlude " An erratic intruder" by Messrs. A. Blinkburn and Canavan, while Mr. Canavan scored a success with a coon song. Mr. Teddy Whittle fully maintained his reputation as a humorist, his coster sketch being particularly good. Messrs. A. T. Keating and A. Taylor acted as accom- panists. The concert was presided over by Mr. James Dodds and a short address was delivered by the Rev. W. Mellor.

div.head: Up-to-date Fire Places.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Emmanuel Christmas Tree.
div.p: Up-to-date Fire Places.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Emmanuel Christmas Tree.

The sum of £l5 was raised by a Christmas tree held in connection with Emmanuel Reformed Church, on Friday evening. The tree had been erected in the Church Institute, linntsford-road, and its branches were borne down by a heavy load of articles suitable for Christmas presents, which were disposed of by Mr. Harry Bibby who, attired as Santa Claus, pre- sided over the tree.—The opening ceretnony was per- formed by Mr. John Allen, of Liverpool, the Rev. F. Vaughan presiding over a large attendance. - Mr. Allen, in declaring the sale open, said that although business matters had taken him away from Warring- ton to reside, his heart was still with the Reformed Church, in the work connected with which he had spent so many happy years. It seemed to him that history was repeating itself and moving in cycles, as his mind traversed again the past years. This was not the first Christmas tree he had seen erected in that room. This was his first school, the place where he learned those things which best fitted a man for a good citizen and a good Christian. He wished them every success. (Applause,)—Mr. W. Heron moved and Mr. Bibby seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Allen. —The vote was heartily accorded and the sale com- menced. The sale was continued on Saturday, when Mr. Henry Gandy performed the opening ceremony. , A capital concert was given. Various items by Miss Jones, the Emmanuel Male Voice Choir, and Master Tom Barton's Orchestra being included in the pro- gramme. The proceeds will be devoted to the reduc tion of the debt.—A word of praise is due to the Misses Ellen Gandy and Alice and Ahnie Minards, who con- ceived the idea of holding a Christmas tree and who, assisted by their friends, carried out the idea.

Iron Fencing of every description. Lowest prices.—J. S. GARL.tND, 51 to 55, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Order of Druids. The annual meeting of the above Order (Druids Camp Lodge) was held in the Club room, Higher Angel, Buttermarket-street on Saturday night the 16th inst. The Officer's present irmluded Bro. Thomas Jones in the chair. Bro. John Flaherty occupying the vice chair, D.G.M. Wm. Hankey, John Woods and D.L. Robert Perdue. After initiating several new members the Chairman called on the D.T. to Present P.D.G.M. Sydney Packer (Lodge Secretary) with a beautifully engraved umbrella. Bro. Perdue in making the presentation . spoke very highly of the manner in which the recipient had discharged the oneious duties of Lodge Secretary. Friendly Society work he said was an entirely voluntary performance and working men made many sacrifices of time in con- nection with it. Daring the lengthy period he had been associated with the Order of Druids he had never known a Bro. who had been more energetic in furthering the interest of the Society and it was with the greatest pleasure that he found himself in the position Ile was ;in that night: In conclusion be said hb joined most !heartily with the other members of the Lodge in wish- ing Bro. Packer long -.life and health to use it. Hankey and D.D.G.11. John Woods , expressed feelingly their pleasure in being present that evening. Bro. Packer responded in a few words thanking them for the presentation and assuring them that he would endeavour to do his duty in the future as he had done in the past. A rote of thanks was accorded the district officers for their services andlhe remainder of the evening was given over to harmony Some good songs being rendered in capital style, ana not until the inexorable call of " time please," did the meeting disperse and a very enjoyable evening cane to a close.

The will of the late Mr. Peter Stubs, .of Blaisdon Hall, Newnham, Severn, the late Gloucestershire High Sheriff (and formerly of Statham Lodge, near Lyrom), has been proved at Gloucester at under £452,729. Visit of Dyson's Gipsy Choir. The inhabitants of Warrington. and district will hail with pleasure the return of Dyson's Gipsy Choir and Dioramas during the Christmas holidays and opening on Sunday next with a Pictorial Sacred Service at 8.15 at the Parr Hall. The excellence of their ! entertainments is quite a household word and they are bright, crisp and up-to--date. The programme is ! changed at every performance and includes pictures, music and sketches. " A tour round the world " is announced for Christmas night at 8 and two enter- tainments will be held on Boxing Day afternoon at 3 " London to Lands End " and evening at 8 " Old Ireland." The Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes have just made their award of the W. Lockett Agnew's' Art Cmnpetition for 1905. One of the prize winners in group 2 (Mechanical or Architectural , drawing) is Mr. Isaac A. Simpson, a student at the ' above-named school, whose miniature of Frodsham Parish Church was awarded the first place by the examiners, thair comment upon the work being "very neatly executed." div.head: CHRISTMASTIDE. PREPARATIONS FOR LOCAL
div.p: CHRISTMASTIDE. PREPARATIONS FOR LOCAL
FESTIVITIES.

Were it not for the lavishness of the shop window displays, it would be almost difficllt to realize that Christmastide is so near at hand. Ihe mildness of the weather during the past few days has dispelled all hope of an "old-fashioned "Christmas unless a change sets in at theeleventh hour. The appearance of the streets, however, affords striking indications of the approach of the great festival. Tradespeople have vied with one another in setting out their splendid stocks of seasonable goods in the most tempting way, and the windows have probably never looked more attractive. There is every reason to believe that Christmas will be cele- brated by Warringtonians with the usual hearti- ness, and there will be few homes to which the joys of the season will not penetrate in some degree, however remote. At the various public institutions every effort is being exerted to make the day a memorable one. An "Examiner" representative who visited the Workhouse on Thursday found the work of decorating the large dining hall in full swing. Evergreens, mottoes, &c., are being utilized so as to produce a very pretty effect and on Christman Day the room will present a cheerful and animated appearance. The Inarmary too has been very tastefully embellished, and each ward has some reminder of the festive time. There will be no lack of festivities to cheer the inmates of the Workhouse on Christmas Day. After divine ser- vice in the morning dinner will be served. The inmates will be free to spend the afternoon pleasantly, and there will be a "special " tea. The concluding event of the day will be an impromptu smoking concert. Some idea of the extent of the catering will be gained from the following particulars of the food which has been ordered :-4701b5.1 beef ; 701bs. suet ; IGOlbs. currants ; 1001bs. raisins ; 1001bs. sultanas ; 8 !lbs. candied peel. In addition 4000zs, of tobacco will dis- appear in smoke, and 61ozs. of snuff wiil be provided for the old men. There will be mineral waters and beer for those who desire them, and four cases of oranges and four barrels of apples will be distributed. Xmas is always an exceptionally busy time at the Post Office and elaborate arrangements have been mule to cope with the traffic. The Gymnasium is being used for parcel post services and the Conservative Assembly Rooms for town postmen's deliveries during the week end. An extra staff will be employed both on the in- door work and collection duties. The public is re- quested to post as early as possible.

div.head: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT. Another Great Success.
div.p: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT. Another Great Success.

When the annual concerts in connection with People's College were revived six years ago, the depar- ture was hailed with pleasure by the many friends of this honoured school, and complete success was confi- dently predicted. Expectations have not been belied for, stimulated by cordial public appreciation, teachers and scholars have entered into the projects with such enthusiasm that People's College concert is now looked forward to as one of the most enjoy- able events of the musical season. Its increas- ing popularity was evidenced in a marked degree by the crowded attendance at the Parr Hall on Thursday evening when the scholars presented an enter- tainment which fully upheld the high standard created by previous efforts. It was indeed pleasing to note the interest manifested b 5 such a large assembly, while the bright faces of the children on the platform betokened their delight at figuring on this most memorable of occasions in the school year. The programme was in every way admirable,the most varied tastes being catered for. There were patriotic choruses, sea songs which went with a capital swing, pleasing solos; and items of the most humorous description, while a complete change was afforded in the shape of a little Shakespearean acting. The opening chorus "Red, White and Blue" was given with fine verve, and the item which followed—" The Death of Nelson"—was particularly appropriate in this the year of the Trafalgar Centenary. Without further particularising, it may be stated that all the choruses were intelligently and expressively interpreted and called forth warm approval. The choice of soloists again proved a happy oae, for each sang so creditably as to elicit an encore. Croon Ellam gave "Three for Jack" with its spirited chorus in typical sailor-boy fashion. Florence Bennett had a difficult sow, in "Beyond" but she sang it with taste and expression, the effect being improved by the violin obligato by Dorothy Lawton. Another beautiful song " Dear home songs" which introduced a few lines of several of the old favourites was sweetly interpreted by Louisa Ormiston. One of the greatest successes of the evening was achieved by Ernest Wallington in the laughable song I've got the ooperzootic." He took the part with the utmost self-possession, fully realizing its humorous possibilities, and every word could be dis- tinctly heard. Another scholar who showed himself exceptionally apt in the humorous element was Richard Lawton. He related several stories with irresistible drollery and was rewarded with two encores. Several special features by groups of selected scholars added considerably to the enjoyment. One of the best of these was " Pansy faces "given by Eleanor Woods, who gracefully took the part of tha queen of all the roses" and a number of girls charmingly dressed to represent pansies. The itern,which included a pretty dance, pleased the audience immenselyand a repetition was demanded. Of particular interest was "The song of the fire brigade"written by Mr. C. H. Hands, the second master of the school, and set to music by Mr. W. H. Payton, Mils. Bac. It was presented by u contingent of boys in firemen's uniforms and proved highly success- ful, the boys earning special praise by the precision with which they executed several drills. This was not the only novel feature due to local originality for "The Showman," another of the most acceptable numbers, was written by Miss E. Brown, a member of the teaching stall', while Mr. Payton was responsible for the =sic. T. Tanner was quite at home as the enterprising American showman, and he enter- tained the audience by exhibiting his collection of vvitx-

!works, representing historical characters which were I excellently portrayed by boys and girls. That gallant military company "The Mulligan Guards,"convulsed the audience with their grotesque manoeuvres and recital of their adventures,and a recall was the inevitable result.A ' delightful action song was" Ile Rainbow bridge,"in which several girls acquitted themselves really admirably. It I was a rather hold venture to select she trial scene from "The Merchant of Venice" for presentation at the con- cert but the scholars entrusted with it fulfilled the various roles in a creditable way which disclosed care- ful training. The following appeared :—Portia, Ethel Cooper; Nerissa, Elsie Warren : Duke, Clifford Senior; Antonio, Kenneth Witts ; Bassani°, Thomas G.Thomas; Salarino, George Cawley; Gratiano, Arthur Warburton; Salanio, Thomas Worthington ; Shylock, Stanley Jack- son. First honours were undoubtedly secured by Ethel Cooper who delivered her lines with exceptional dis- tinctness and in aforceful way quite befitting the scene. Stanley Jackson also did extremely well as Shylock, and the other parts were capably sustained. We can- not close this report without congratulating the teach- ing stag on this happy consummation of their efforts, and a meted of praise must be accorded to Mr. IV. H. Payton, Mug. Bas., upon whom the musical training of the scholars largely devolved. He ably presided at the organ and also supplied the pianoforte accompaniments 1 During an enterval Mr. Josiah LoNGLAND, one of I the school managers, briefly congratulated all concerned in the promoticn of the concert specially mentioning the services of Mr. Payton, Miss Brown, Miss Bailey. Miss Wallington, Mr. Hands and Mr. Bowen. He alluded to the school's splendid record and said he was sure that with such an able headmaster and efficient staff the progress of the future would be equally gratifyiog (Applause.) THE COMING ELECTION.

div.head: PROBABLE BATE.
div.p: PROBABLE BATE.

On Wednesday the Cabinet decided to ask the King to dissolve Parliament on January Bth, which will twin,*° the first unopposed borough returns in on the 12th, and the last polls, excepting Orkney and Shet- land, will be over on the 29th. The campaign promises to be unusually general, for already candi- dates are ready in all but a very small percentage of the constituencies. There are a hundred Labour candidates adopted, and in every constituency but three Liberal or Labour representatives have been chdsen, but some thirty-odd remain with Conservative candidates. It is thought probable that the new Parliament will meet on the 13th or 14th of February.

div.p: POLLING DAY IN WARRINGTON.

div.head: LIBERAL POLICY,
div.p: THE LIBERAL POLICY,
The Premier's Pronouncement.

The Prime Minister, on Thursday evening, addressed a huge audience in the Albert Hall, London, and, in speaking of the Liberal policy respecting India, said the new Government would make themselves party to no invasion of the great principle of the subordination of the military to the civil authority. Respecting South Africa, the Government had resolved to stop forthwith the recruitment and embarkation of coolies from China in- to South Africa until the opinion of a representative Government of the colony could be had, and instruc- tions had been already given to this effect. The exist- ing friendship with France would be cordially main- tained. He believed there were fresh sources of taxa- tion to be tapped, such as the land and licences. Mili tarisrn, extravagance and Protection were weeds that grew in the same field, and must all be cut out. The country would never have been confronted with the spectre of Protection if it ' had not been for the South African war. The Govern- ment believed in self-government and popular control. What other than this, he asked, was the foundation of our Irish policy, that these domestic affairs which con- cerned the Irish people only and not ourselves should be placed in their hands ? The issue of the next general election was fixed, and could not be altered by Mr., Balfour.

div.head: TRADES DISPUTE BILL.
div.p: TRADES DISPUTE BILL.
Government's Promise.

The Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Unions Congress, on Thursday, had an interview with the Prime Minister, who was accompanied by the Lord Chancellor, in reference to the Trades Dispute Bill. The deputation was introduced by Mr. Cummings: chairman of the Parliamentary Committee, and Mr. Shackleton, M.P., and Mr. Bell, M.P., spoke on their behalf.

Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, in reply, admitted the urgency of the matter, and promised that a bill on the general lines of the Parliamentary Committee should be introduced at an early date, and without any unnecessary delay.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION.
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION.
Conservative Meeting at Padgate. COLONEL PILKINGTON " HECKLED."

A meeting called by the Conservatives was held on Wednesday evening in the schoolroom at Padgate,alarge audience assembling. Mr. George Mather presided. The chief speakers were Colonel Pilkington, the member, and Alderman Bennett. The meeting was orderly, but there were at times some very lively passages which the audience enjoyed. The Colonel was prevailed upon to stop, for it was pointed out that at a previous meeting he had run away to catch a train " before questions could be put to him. _ _
Several members of the audience, notably Mr. E. England and Mr. George Walker, who is a member of the Education Committee in Warrington, thereupon "heckled" the Colonel.

The first named took him up upon German Tariffs, , upon which he had been speaking.—Mr. England asked how it was, if Protection was such a" good thing" that ! the German p9ople were crying out for more Free Trade and demonstrated this by reading out certain clauses in the new German Tariff which becomes law in March 1900, Whereby all steam boilers—machinery— mechanical appliances &c., made abroad for ships shall be admitted free—as also shall all vessels and ships made abroad required for commercial purposes." Mr. George Walker asked whether Colonel Pilking- ton upheld the Education Act which prevented teachers from being admitted into the !Training Colleges and 15,000 schools, without a religious test. Other gentlemen raised the Chinese Labour Question which Colonel Pilkington had severely left alone in his speech, but Colonel Pilkington only answered this by asking questions himself and asked what would the Liberal Party do with the Chinese in South Africa?" NIL England replied " Send them home again." There were several workingmen there who evidently had followed Mr. Pilkington's method of voting in the House—for they asked him why he gave certain votes, which adversedly affected the workingmen. Colonel Pilkington adroitly answered by making speeches, but it took him fully half an hour to do so for he paid his audience the compliment by saying it had shown itself to be an exceptionally intelligent one. ' —The meeting did not break up until close upon 10 o'clock.

div.head: KNUT,,SFORD DIVISION. The Liberals Adopt Mr. King.
div.p: KNUT,,SFORD DIVISION. The Liberals Adopt Mr. King.

Lest Saturday a special meeting of the General Coun- cil of the Kuutsford Division Liberal Association was held in King-street, Manchester "to hear an address from Mr. Alfred J. King, with a view to his adoption as the Liberal candidate for the above division at the next general election." Lord Stanley of Alderley pre- sided over a good attendance, which included Messrs. W. Madden, J. Kenworthy, Grapeenhall ; J. Bittersby, Lower Walton ; E. Lloyd Jones, Stockton Heath ; and C. Jackson Holmes, Latchford .Without, _ _

Mr. H. Roberts v'erote : "Whatever I can do for Mr. King I shall have the greatest pleasure in doing. Hoping for a big 'win' all round." Mr. Greg moved: "That this meeting of the General Council is of opinion that Mr. A. J. King is a fit and proper person to represent the Knutsford Division of the county of Chester in Parliament, and pledges itself to use every legitimate means to secure his return to the House of Commons." Mr. Madden supported the resolution on behalf of the Grappenhall pollingdistrict. He was glad to state that there were three or four gentlemen in the room who did not quite agree with the view expressed that the Liberal Unionist Free Traders were going back. At any rate, it was not the case in the Grappenhall district. Alluding to the appeal made to sink small differences, Mr. Madden said he was a Catholic and an Irishman, and to him there were qnes- tions dearer than life, but he was prepared to sink big differences—(hear, hear)—and though he was an Irish- man and a Home Ruler, under the banner of Liberalism and freedom there was room for all. (Applause.) Mr. Lloyd Jones assured the meeting that at Stockton i Heath they had no hesitation n pledging themselves to , work night and day, if necessary, to return Mr. King at the head of the poll. They were paying special attention to those who had no opinions wikatever, because they were the people who would turn, and it behoved them to be on the alert and assist them to make up their minds in favour of Free Trade and Liberalism. He believed that Mr. King would pledge himself to vote with and consistently follow the leader of the Liberal Party, and they in Stockton Heath believed that the right man and the right men were in the right places. (Hear, hear). ' Messrs. Godwrad, Fletcher, Hayes, Burgess, Aidley and Owen also supported the resolution, which was carried.

div.head: "THE CRICKET ON THE HEARTH." --- Dramatic Performances at Messrs. Crosfields'.
div.p: "THE CRICKET ON THE HEARTH." --- Dramatic Performances at Messrs. Crosfields'.

7,lessrs. Crosffelds' Amateur Dramatic Society can now be regarded as a permanent and welcome addition to the entertainment organizations in connection with the works. Inaugurated twelve months ago the first piece to be presented was not one which taxed to a great extent the abilities of the performers but the same cannot be said of " The Cricket on the Hearth " which was produced on Wednesday. It is unnecessary to enter into a description of the drama which is an adaptation of the old and well-known story told by Charles Dickens. From a performer's point of view, however, a more trying piece for a young amateur society could hardly be selected. From beginning to end there is none of that subtle humonr so often associated with I)icken'3 works to brighten a pathetic story and the play suffers. to a certain .extent, from this want of contrast. The players, however, all rose to the occasion end entered into their work with spirit. Mr. J. W. Spensley carried off the palm as Caleb Plummer, an old toy maker. Displaying a perfect control over his voice and actions he showed a close and effective study of the part. John Perryhingle was excellently portrayed by Mr. G. B. Dean though there was a slight want of harmony in his work, and too rapid a transition from mirth to anger. Mr. .1. E. Newnes' acting was, generally, forceful as Mr. 'Tacklaton. Mr. W. Tynan had little to do as the son of Caleb Plummer. but that little he did well. Miss E. Darbyshire made an excellent and homely wife to John Perrybingle, and rose to the occasion admirably when her innocent but misguided actions cause her. husband to suspect her constancy. Miss S. Darybyshire as the blind daughter of the toy maker had a part full of difficulty, the spirit of which she however, fully realized. Miss E. Wright (Mrs. Fielding), Miss L. Pooley (May Fielding), Miss N. Thomason (Tilley Slowboy), and Miss h. Cank (the spirit of the cricket) tilled parts of a minor character with success. On the whole the drama was excellently staged, and should encourage the Society to greater efforts. "The Cricket on the Hearth " was preceded by an amusing farce "Ted on Perla Francais " in which the characters were ably unstained by Mr. G. B. Dean (Major Pattan), Nfr. E. IV. Warren (victor Dubois), Mr. I'. E. Gartland (Mr. Spriggins), Miss S. Darby shire (Angelina), Miss .l. Arstrong (wife of Major Patton), and Miss E. Wright (maid-of-all-work). During the evening instrumental items were given by the works orchestra under the conductorship of Mr. Lord. The performance was repeated on Thursday when, as on Wednesday evening, there was a crowded audience the Assembly Room.

div.head: LUDWIG CONCERT.
div.p: THE LUDWIG CONCERT.

It was a matter for surPrise and regret that the enter- prise of the Catholic Young Men's Society in arrang- ing for the visit of Mr. William Ludwig, the famous baritone to Parr Flail on Monday evening was not. better rewarded. The attendance was not nearly so large as the excellence of the entertainment warranted and one has a difficulty in accounting for the unresponsiveness of the public. For many years Ludwig has been a popular figure on the stage and concert platform its turn, and be still retains his hold on the esteem of music- lovers. Of erect bearing, he has a striking platform presence while it is evident to all who hear him that he throws himself heart and soul into his singing. On Monday he was accorded a hearty reception and delighted the audience with characteristic interpreta- tions of no fewer than eight songs. Some of them were quaint Irish melodies with their alternating notes of pathos and fire and Mr. Ludwig sang them in a way which appealed to all. Two of the choicest items, given by reqnest, were Gounod's "There is a Green Hill,' and " Nazareth," and Mr. Ludwig infused much feeling into his renderings. Miss Winifred Rose Ludwig sang "Coo "from the Country Girl " and " The mild plaid shawl " with taste, and Miss Florence Ludwig very sweetly interpreted "Once" and "Come back to Erin." Mr. Tames Foye possesses nure-toned tenor voice and the audience were loud in their eppreciation of his expressive render- ings of "When other lips" and " Sweet vales of Arklow." Mr. George Potter gave flute soles in accomplished style, and some clever Irish <lances by Miss Rose Moran proved popular features. Mr. James Geraghty crated no little amusement with hi R Trish fireside stories. The appearance of sevoral local artistes gave considerable pleasure to the assembly. Mr. J. W. Bibby sang" Down in the deep" with such effeet as to call forth no encore, and he res- ponded with " The Yeoman's Wedding." The voices of Messrs. Peter end J. M. Bate blended well in two duets which were cordially received. MSS Florence Ludwig was an able accompanist.

div.head: EARL PERCY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: EARL PERCY AT WARRINGTON.
RETALIATION ADVOCATED.
Criticism of Mr. Outhwaitc.

A Conservative mass meeting was held in the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening, the principal speaker being Earl Percy, ALP., under secretary for foreign affairs in the late administration. There was a large attendance, presided over by Sir Gilbert reenall, Bart. The hall had been lavishly decorated with flags and party mottoes. . _ .

In the course of his address Earl Percy said that he I was invited a fortnight ago to address a Lancashire audience, for the first time in support of the Govern- : meat. He was sorry it was quite impossible for him to redeem his promise in that respect. (Lsughter.) He i could not pretend to feel the slightest confidence in the Government which was now responsible for the con- I duct of the affairs of the country. His whole confidence was reserved for the Government of whieh, until lately j he was a humble member, and which, almost for twenty years, with only three years' interval, had enjoyed the unbroken support of the great majority of the elector- ate of this country. He did not pretend that the Government had not made mistakes but he considered , that for the record of their administration and legisla- tion and above all, of their foreign policy, they : I deserved well of the country. So successful had been ; the foreign pike, of the late Government I that he observed their opponents were very i anxious to persuade them that the advent of the ; Radical party to power would involve no breach in the continuity of that policy. Idu not know," Earl Percy said, whether that I assurance, satisfactory as it id, carries conviction to the minds of anybody present. 'confess it carries none, to mine. We are asked to place our reliance in a small , : body, unhappily, of three or four gentlemen who call ; themselves Liberal Imperialists, ane who sit in a Cabinet composed almost entirely, or very largely, of avowed' Little Englanders,' presided over by a Prime Minister who, during the South African war, did not ! scruple to endorse—l have no doubt he fully believed in them—many of thenccusations made on the Continent against not only oar policy but against the conduct of I I our troops. I dare say in this Cabinet the Liberal I Imperialists may to a certain extent control the Prime Minister, I daresay the tail will wag the dog, but that . is not the principle which hitherto the people of this country have liked to see ebeir Government follow." Earl PEECY dealt at some length with the question of Home Rule. Sir IL Campbell-Bannerman had explained what his policy in regard to Ireland was, supposing the, Liberals were returned to power. It was that they were , going to introduce a number of Bills, all of which were to be consistent with, and were to lead up to the larger policy, which ceremended itself to the Irish Nationalist i Party. Well, they turned to the Irish Nationalist ! Party to know what that larger policy was, and Mr. Redmond, only a few days after Sir H. Campbell- Bannerman had made his speech, re-asserted that the Irish Nationalste would he content, with nothing less , than a separate Parliament for Ireland,with an executive' responsiole to it. There might be a certain number of electors, and always would be, who were tired of an administration which had held office for as long a period ' as ten years uninterruptedly, and who would like to see a change, but he did not believe that the great mass of the people had changed one iota in their destation and abhorence of separation for Ireland. (Applause). The SPEAKER next alluded to the Chinese labour question. It was vital they should krow what the intentions of the Radical Patty were on the question— vital to South Africa because without an adequate labour simply the mines could not, be worked, and the withdrawal of the labour supply meant practically the ruin of South Africa. It was vital to us for two , reasons. We had sunk an enormous amount of money: in the country—he was not talking of capitalists' money and the money invested in the mines—we had I invested twenty millions of the taxpayers' money in al loan to the Transvaal, and unless the industries of South' Africa could he revived, it was impossible for us to! ever get a penny of that back. It was also vital because there were already a great number of white men ! —20,000 as against 15,000 before the Chinese were intro- duced—employed in the Transvaal, and melt were pre- ! paring to start everyday for that country, and they had a right to know whether by one adruinistrative Act they were to be deprived of employment and pros- ; Deets of employment which had been held out to them. f As to the reasons which influenced the late Government : in sanctioning the ordinance, it was not that they I thought the introduction of Chinese labour in itself was a very desirable policy. It was that having care- I fully examined every possible alternative they believed ! that no other coarse was open to them. Teat white I men could or would or ought to work in the mines in, South Africa side by side with blackruen no one who ! had the slightest first-hand knowledge of South Africa ; had ever dared to assert. Mr. Creswell, of the Village ! !slain Reef Mine, tried the employment of whites as unekilled labourers and the experiment proved an entire failure both financially and from a social point of view. Nobody who professed to know any- thing about South Africa, had ever made the assertion that the mines could be worked by white labour except Mr. Outhwaite, Mr. Chamberlain's opponent, who some time ago visited Warrington. Mr. Outhwaite was under the impressionthat South Africa was an entire exception in the whole of the British Empire, and that in every other colony mining work was done by whites. Had Mr. Outhwaite never heard of India, where the mines were worked entirely by natis es, or the Straits Settle- ment., or Singapore, where the mines were worked almost entirely by Chinese or British Guiana,where the work in the extensive plantations was done by imported coolies under an ordinance sanctioned by the Liberal Party—(applause)—and almost identical in its provisions with the ordinance eassed for South Africa. There was notn single cobany probably in the whole of the British Empire where mines were worked by white labour except Canada and 'Australia both of which colonies differed radically and essentially in the elementary con- citions of the problem horn South Africa. [ley could dismiss the idea that whites could do the unskilled work in the mines if allowed. Whites could do the skilled work, but they could only do it if from other sceurces unskilled workers were suppliel Mr. Outhwaite was under the impression that the Kaffir was the more expensive article than the Chinese. As a matter of fact the Chinese were far better workers than Kielfirs, but the cost of the Chinese labourers including the wages and the co3t of bringing them out there and send- ing them back was larger than that of Kaffir labour. Kaitirs had been imported hem British Centrel Africa and tried,but they could not stand the climate:lnd died in large numbers:The only reason they preferred the Chinese was that there mei not sufficient Kaffir !abortr available, and that Kaffir labour could only be employed at the cost of a great loss of life. Every precaution had been taken from the point of view of the interests of the working classes and of the Chivamau himself. If the Radicals allowed the ordinance to remain in force, it would be a confession either that they had made the most odious charge that could be made—that of per- mitting slavery under the British. flag—which had no foundation in fact ; or else, believing that it was true when they came Into power for sheer lack of moral courage they were going to continuo in force a system they themselves believed to be immoral. (Loud applause.) Earl Percy continuing snid the country had a right to expect that the new Government would do something to encourage trade. Upon that point there was a clear and sharp issue betwe, en the two great parties at the . coming election. The Radical party believel; that our fiseal system was absolutely perfect, and that any departure from it, any change, would be a change for the worse. According to the Unionist party our present fiscal system was one of the causes which were respon- sible for the extraordinary fact that it did not matter whether trade was going up or down, there were great messes of the, people pernemently almost on the verge of starvation. (Hear, bear.) No one could say we had lost our power of producing cheaply or that we had far greater advantages for cheap production than any of our competitors. Want of employment, therefore, could not he due to any difficulty in the way of cheapness of erode() tiOD. It bad, however, something to do with the difficulty of finding markets. The only reason for that was that our markets were being steadily closed to our goods by foreign tariffs and that at the same time foreign countries were sending their products here, which was the only free market in the world, and selling at below cost price. The whole question was whether it wits worth while to make a change in our fiscal policy—not a great or sensational change, hut a slight change—in order to win hack to ourselves the power of negotiation, which would secnre to us, at all events, fairer treatment in the markets of the world. " You can do that," Earl Percy said. "if you will con- sent to abandon the superstition that there is something intrinsically immoral in ever imposing is duty except for purposes of revenue, no flintier how badly soother country treats our trade, which must always, and under all circumstances, have the free run of the British market. I expect from the adoption of the policy of what is called Retaliation—l have never pre- tended, and I do not think, that it will necessarily have a very great effect in inducing Protectionist countries to lower tariffs which they believe to be absolutely indispensable for the defence of their own industries— that it will place us in a better position to make com- mercial treaties, which you cannot do now. You can- not make a commercial treaty on your own account ; you have to wait till two other nations have made a commercial tieaty between themselves, and then come in under the ' favoured nation ' clause, which,to a large extent, is humbug. (Hear, hear.) Another result of the adoption of a policy of Retaliation is that you will never have to impose a duty at all. The mere know- ledge that you are prepared to use your powers of reprisal will have its effect upon foreign nations." Mr. It. PI ERPOINT, M.P., also addressed the meeting urging " fiscal reform " as a means of binding the Empire.

Warrington Beaten at Dewsbury. Warrington took a strong team to Dewsbury on Saturday, and were expected to return victorious, but they had to submit to defeat by a single point. Fish turned out again after an absence of 3 months, but his value was discounted by the absence of Isherwood. Fine weather prevailed, but there was only an attend- ance of about 6,500. Teams : Dewsbury—Garritty, Fmk ; Bland, Robinson, North- rop, and Evans, three-quarter hacks ; Phillips, Bowen, Cooper, Davies, Matins, Richardson, Sanders, and Thorp, forwards.

Warrington—Knight, lack ; Jordan, Fish, Jones, and Widdeson, three-quarter backs ; Hockenhall and Brooks, half backs ; Preston, Boardman, Shngars, Thomas, Heath, Swift, Jolley, and Naylor, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Salford ; touch judges, Messrs. G. Holdsworth, Halifax ; and F. Morton Castleford. Immediately after the kick-off Warrington were hard pressed. Relief was brought by a penalty kick, but a good rush by the Dewsbury forwards again placed the visitors' line in jeopardy. Robinson evaded Fish in fine style and scored a try, Bowen failing at goal. After both sides had attacked la turn Preston received the ball from Hockenhall, and breaking through the defence, scored a try which he had no difficulty in converting. Dewsbury were soon on the aggressive again, and Robinson at length got over near the corner flag, but the referee's decision was against him, and the teams crossed over with two points in favour of Warrington. Phillips restarted, and Dewsbury at once reached their opponents' quarter-line. A tall kick by Knight was misjudged, and the Warrington forwards got away by a combined effort to the Deasbirry quarters. Fish mulling n kick by Bowen enabled Dewsbury to again place the Warrington line in danger, and Carey had an unsuccessful attempt at goal. Some excellent work was next contributed by Robinson, Northrop and Evans, the former being tackled on his opponents' goal-line. Thorp managed to score a try, and Richardson being unsuccessful at goal left Dewsbury the winners by 2 tries (Li points), to 1 goal and 1 try (5 points).

! ADDITIONAL BOOKING PACILITTICS.—The booking (ace which has recently been erected on the "up " side at Sankey Station was opened on Monday. The improve- ment was necessary and will be a great convenience to the travelling public. Carctua CLUB DANCC.—A dance and whist drive in connection with the Penketh Cricket Club were held on ' Friday evening in the Great Sankey Sunday schools. ' About 90 persons were present. Ths music was supplied by Messrs. J. and W. Ray. The duties of .M.C.'s were ' efficiently carried out by Mr. T. E. Shoobridge and Mr. George Kirkham, whilst the catering was in the hands of Mrs. George Clarke. In the whist drive Mr. H. Cartwright, son., was successful in winning the ' gentleman's prize (a beautiful inkstand) and Miss Hettio • Edgerley won the lady's prize. The following gentle- ; men carried out the arrangements in as very creditable manner :—Messrs. Herbert Davies (secretary), A. Boardman, A. Hodgkinson, T. E. Shoobrid,ge, F. Ward, George Kirkham, E. Foster, and F. Dumbill.

Warrington P.S.A. Society. There was a large attendance at the weekly meeting of the above society on Sunday. Councillor Stott pre- sided and in a'short address on "The true aim of life." stated that the only aim some people seemed to have in life was to win the " sweep ' on the football match or horse race. lie regretted this growth of the gambling evil. It was becoming a greater evil than the drink question. The only true aim was to uplift the fallen, end endeavour to make life bright and better for our fellows. Mr. A. E. Elliott was the speaker. He urged each one present to be true to the very highest and made a plea for a broader spirit and a nore widened outlook than Warringtonians seemed to have. Mr. P. Dendy read the Scripture lesson, and Mr. B. Wadsworth and the President (Mr, Wynne Jones) also took part in the meeting.

div.head: WALKING DAY.
div.p: WALKING DAY.
PROPOSAL TO ALTER THE DATE.
Discussion at the Education Committee Meeting.

IFrom time to time efforts have been made to bring about an alteration in the date of Warrington's annual Walking Day but these have all failed. Recently the Warrington Tradesmen's Association approached the Educutiou Committee with a view to their revising the ' date of the children's festival and at their meeting on Monday the Education Committee were asked by the School Attendance Committee to fix NVallriug Day for the Friday proceeding August Monday and to arrange ; that the school summer holidays commence on that date.

Councillor EaISON moved the adoption of the recommendation. Mr. MAY seconded. No doubt the Committee were all aware of the difficulties which had from time to time arisen and the number of meetings which had been held in order to try and find a satisfactory day for Walking Day. They Irtd considered the letters from the fradesmen's Association and of the injury done to education by the bad attendance and confusion caused by the present date of the festival and the multiplication of days for holidays. They had also considered the difficulties the various churches had had, and bad been assured by the representative of one large body that the Friday before August Monday would be a satisfactory date. Mr. UPSON asked if the Committee were hound by the resolution. The resolution meant that, the school holidays should bo practically the whole of the month of August. If the Committee were going to be bound he %could move an amendment.
Alderman BENNETT : I suppose the Committee would be bound.

Mr. lire()); : Then I prepose that the minute . be not confirmed. Continuing, he said he did so for two reasons. Ho was somewhat amazed at the light-hearted recklessness of the Corn-! mittee ire attacking such an old institution as the War- rington Walking Day. Walking Day was practically fixed by the Suuday schools,and was the day of days in Warrington. In proposing to alter the date of Walking Day, they were legislating for a large number of people. It was a well-known fact that perhaps 70 per cent, of the children of the town were fitted out with summer clothing for Walking Day, end they knew that if it were not for the great festival there were children in the borough who would not get a proper fit-out in the matter of summer clothing. If the date was made later many parents would not fit out their children with summer clothing at the fag end of the season. He thought that fact had I not been suificiently grasped by the Committee. but had been lost sight of. It was suggested that the school slimmer holidays should be held during the month of August. Sea-side places and torrists resorts were conjested during Augnst and appeals had been made to such bodies as the Education Committee, who had the power to arrange the holidays, to hold them earlier in the year. So far in Warrington they had had half of the holidays in July and it had been a compara- tively easy matter to obtain accommodation at those places during the first fortnight. The committee em- ployed hetween 300 and 409 people and those people were not large wage earners—probably the average income would he below £loo—and surely they were entitled to some consideration. The proposal of the School Attendance Committee was discnseed at a meeting of teachers the previous Saturday and he was asked to bring the matter before the Committee and to point out that the teachers were unanimous in asking that the holidays should not be so Laces the month of August. It was very much more expensive to have the holidays in August than earlier in the year. Mr. FAIRCLOWAI said there was a good deal in what , Mr. Ues-ox seid on behalf of the children. 'There was ! no doubt that if it were not for Walking Day a good many children would not get fresh and good clo;hing. He thought that if they altered the date of Walkingl Day as suggested they would make a mess of it. Mr. PrexsroN hoped that the principal ground of the ' mover of the amendment was not that of the effect , upon the teachers which an alteration in the date of Walking Day would have. That was not the proper way to consider the question. The resolution it carried simply meant that Walking Day would be a month later ! and the summer holidays would commence nine or ten , days later. It had been stated by Mr. Upson that a greet, many children get clothing once a year. Mr. UPSON : I said nothing of the sort. Mr, PLINSTON : You said they were rigged out once a year. Mr. UesoN . I said nothing of the sort. Mr. PLINSTON continuing said he was going to argue that the holding of Walking Day one month later would make no difference in regard to the children getting clothing. Moreover at the end of July there; was a greater chance of the weather being more settled than ot the end of June. By the proposed alteration the , break at the end of June would be done away with and parents of the children would have a longer holiday at the beginning of August, Mr. limey pointed' out that the committee were not unanimous in their recommendation. He would like to know if the Educetion Committee had any power ,! with respect to the fixing of Walking Day. Alderman 111:NNETT : We have no power, but our representation would probably have great weight. The Rev. Father WILSON said it seemed to him very , desirable that Walking Day and school holidays should he brought together. The suggestion before the committee did not by any means I exhaust the possible alternatives which might be submitted. It might be found possible to bring Walking Day a little later and the school holidays a little earlier. A great many parties were interested in the suggestion, and he thaught the difficulty couldl he very well met by being referred to a sub-committee whn could go more widely into the matter. Mr. H. ROWARTS thought there wets DO need to be afraid or the Committee binding Itself to anything. In the whole of his experience he never saw the adminis- tration of public affairs in the town lend itself se complacently to whet it considered a change of opinion. They passed a resolution to-day and immediately to-morrow upset it, and passed one entirely opposite. If Mr. Upson would only persevere there was plenty of time between that night and when it was necessary to , give an absolutely definite opinion as to what the policy of the town would be, and he would guarantee that before the matter was finally settled many in that room would change their minds two or three times. (Laughter.) 1, The Mevoa thought that in regard to Walking, Day it was best to let well alone, and to leave the matter as it stood. Councillor LORD expressed himself in favour of ' Walking Day being fixed for a later date. Councillor FULTON SMITH said the date of the festival had been the cause of a great deal of discussionl in years gone by, nnd he thought a very strong case had been made out why the present day should be fixed. Some of the large works in town fixed their stock-taking for the end of June and than men were allowed a week's holiday. Walking Day fitted in with that arrangment. If walking Day was fixed for a later date the attend- ance at school would still suffer onnccount of the works being closed. . Councillor Evetee said there was an old saying that ," wise men change their minds but fools never." (Laughter). I Mr. ROBERTS : I would like to correct my friend. Some wise men change their minds. (Laughter). Councillor EVANS : I only quoted the old saying did not want anyone to apply it. (Laughter). Contin- uing, he said he believed the tradesmen of the town had moved in the matter because of the fact that they had so many broken holinays which were injurious to busi- ness and meant considerable loss. The tradesmen viewed the question in the light that by the proposals before the Committee they would be giving all workmen a fair and reasonable holiday and would prevent some of the broken time which they bed at present. He did not think Mr. Upson was quite so selfish in advocating a cause es he had been that night. His standpoint was absolutely selfish. There were men in that room who bed a great deal of coosideratiou and. kindly feeling for the children who were apparently helpless, and realized what Walking Day meant for them. The primary factor in Mr. Upton's argument had been with respect to economic conditions of the poorly paid teaching staff in the town. Mr. UPSON : I deny emphatieally that T used such a 'word as poorly paid. I don't think Mr. Evans has any right to put into my mouth words which I never need. Councillor EVANS : You said teachers considered they could get 'holidays more economically before August than during August. You pleaded from an absolutely selfish itanpoi»t for the teachers. Continu- ing Councillor Evans supported the recommendation. He pointed out that by holding Walking Day on the Friday before August Monday parents would have four days' holiday. They would be forced to take certain holidays in August even if the recommendations were not approved, and would also take a holiday at the end of June. Consequently there was a considerable loss in wage earning and therefore from the parents' standpoint the alteration would be a saving. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said he could not help expressing

regret that Councillor Evans should accuse Mr. Upson of selfishness. Although be was elected on the com- mittee to represent the teachers it was only fair to say in the plainest possible terms that he had in the most honourable and straightforward way refrained at all times from doing anything which might be in the least degree suggested as grinding the axes of teachers. Mr. Jolley pointed out that a year ago the committee re- arranged the holidays to meet the difficulty formerly caused by the breaks at Easter and Whitsuntide and the grants did not therefore suffer by diminished averages through an odd day coming in. This was not merely a tradesmen's or a teachers' question, but a town's question. There were a great many interests to be considered and particularly the interests of the great works of the town. The present day, he under- stood, was fixed upon as meeting the wishes of the majority. He believed the organizers of the works excursions were able to secure better accommodation by having those trips on a day which should not clash with tiled Bank Holiday traffic. The stocktaking at several works was also arranged for that time. He suggested that the committee would not lose anything by supporting the amendment, not with the view of expressing a definite opinion as to which day was the best, but simply that the whole question wanted full cepsideratiou and they ought not to take action which would seem to commit them.

Canon MORLEV STEVENSON said the question was a very complex one, affecting the interests of many people. He thought, however, that the committee should look at everything from the point of view of Education. They had nr, power to fix Walking day but if there was going to be any change it would be within their power to matte representations and he trusted they would make thee:. from the educational point of view. Ho would like to emphasise what struck him as the most valuable suggestion which fell from Father Wilsm. Surely it would not be outside the points of possibility to" tack" Walking Day onto some holiday. Everyone could see that it was educationally wrong that the Committee should be giving too frequent holidays. Councillor WILKINSON thought that if the present date was suitable for the stock-taking arrangements at the works it should not be altered.

The CHAIRMAN thought Father Wilson's suggestion offered the basis of a satisfactory solution. Councillor ELIASON said the matter was first brought forward in consequence of a strong representation made to him by a number of workingmen that the .holidays should be altered. They pointed out that it • was im- possible for them to go away for holidays and take their children at the present time of Walking Day as school's were opened as usual the next week. On a vote being taken the amendment WAS defeated. Mr. PmNsToN : I see that the seconder of the minutes (Mr. May) has voted against them. (Laughter).

THE MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
" St. John's Eve."

- - At the Musical Society's concert in Parr Hall on Wednesday evening a small audience enjoyed a concert which it is no exaggeration to say merited, if it did not secure, the attention of a thousand of our laggardly musical public. Mr. F. H. Cowen's cantata " St. John's Eve " formed the staple item in the pro- gramme, and it became early apparent that the audience were deeply and pleasurably interested in tire work. The cantata is in point of fact, a dainty and altogether charming production, its foundation story of Bennett's poem embodying an English idyll, the pastoral and lyrical beauties of which at once appeal to the sense of the listener. Anti despite the fact that a studied simplicity characterises the work as a musical com- position, there is no doubt that in the 15 years that have elapsed since its first production, it has attained as it was early seen to deserve, a position ranking with the ablest of our English works. The society's chorus experienced no serious difficulty in presenting the choral portions of" St. John's Eve,' which include some very attractive numbers of a peculiarly picturesque and dramatic order suggestive of light opera rather than the more restrained cantata. The ensemble choruses were invariAbly good, as were also those pertions of the other choruses in which the male voices are separately massed. Only in places where the ladies are heard alone and together were 'there one or two obscurities and timid entries. The vigorous opening of the chorus "Ho ! good St. John was a I shining light" with its well defined therne,oft recurring in course of the work, may be cited an instance of this ' excellence in the male section of the chorus, while the concluding portion of the opening chorus "Bring branches "—otherwise sung most spiritedly—may be mentioned as illustrating the slight failure alluded to. Around the first mentioned chorus it is that such difficulty as the work presents centres. Yet its kaleidoscopic Ahanges of picturesque animation were splendidly brOught out,the contrast of the strong vocal parts attending the depicting of the wild dance around the burning pile, with the soothing harmonies of the concluding portion announcing to all " A sweet good night " being worthy of all praise. It is gratifying to note that the society was able to find in its ranks a capable exponent of the principal part of " Margaret ' in the person of Miss Nellie Anderton who is, we understand, undergoing a thorough training as a contralto vocalist. The manner of her renciering of the often onerous music allotted to this part is full of the promise of great possibilities. Miss Anderton most intelligently emphasised the dramatic features surrounding the character of the "ancient dame "whose soothsayings form the introductory basis lof the libretto, and in the air " You Nancy at the night's full moon " as in the carol "Three Kings onced liv'd," she so far achieved success that the audience would fain have listened to repetitions had circum- stances permitted. Miss Hilda d'Angelis made, if we ! mistake not, her local debut at this concert. In the part of "Nancy" she was most happily placed, her bright and delicately flexible soprano voice and graceful style eminently fitting her for its impersonation. A conspicu- ous charm was noticable in her singing of that part of the aria " 0 peaceful night " commencing" 0 what does't thou bear ?" which, with its wealth of easily flowing melody, she made the most of. Associated with Mr. Henry Brearley. —who ably vocalised the tenor part of" The Young Squire "—in the duet" Fairest of roses," Miss D'Angelis displayed a reserve of deep feeling which artistically enhanced this climacteric point of the cantata. By Mr. Brearley and Mr. James Coleman the principal tenor and bass parts were presented with marked taste. The part of the derided" Robert" (the boastful lover) though rather is thankless one, contains passages demanding musicianly qualities which Mr. Coleman at all times showed he possessed. A splendid love-song "0 Zephyr stirring 'midst the leaves,"—the theme of which in a representative phrase is effectively regenerated in other portions of the work,—falls to the lot of the principal tenor, and scored as it is with a harp accompaniment alone,it afforded Mr. Brearley a fine opportunity of which he took full 'advantage, of displayiug a fine voice and a good style. • The cantata depends largely for the realisation of its many delicate and faucitul details, as for its more massive proportions,upen an orchestra of 4igh efficiency especially in the wood wind and the horn sections to whom are entrusted sonic, charming effects. Though necessarily somewhat involved the orchestral parts are really not difficult and Mt Wednesday they were played with uniform precision and good taste. Altogether a very pleasing impression remains of this performance of" St. John's Eve "heard again in War- rington after an interval of many years. The second part of the programme contained the overture to " Micelle" (Gototo.1), the choral part-song 'The gallant Troubadour" ( Watson), aud a song each for the principal vocalists each and all of whom were, with some enthusiasm in turn recalled. Miss .d'Augelis's choice of the " Solveig's song" (Grieg) was exactly suited to her voice and style. Making no exigent deniands upon the vocalist it was yet warbled forth with so charming an earnestness us to win all hearts, appro- priate response to an encore being made with Carey's graceful " Pastoral." Miss Anderton is to be congratu- lated upon pluckily undertaking the exacting song "Softly awakes my heart" (Saint Samar) with orchestra. The magnificent breadth of its melody and the strong dramatic feeling embodied in the text of this operatic excerpt form a tempting bait to ambitions singers. That Miss Anderton largely realised its possibilities with the audience was shown in the persistent demand for u repetition which followed her rendering of it. Although the quality of Miss Anderton's voice in its upper part is singularly round and ' mellow, it is distinctly deficient in 'volume in the lower register, a temporary defect which the maturing influence of time, along with assiduous training, may confidently be expected to make good. And in thus applying herself to further study Miss Anderton may be assured of the hest wishes of her townspeople. Mr. Brearley's ssng " The sailor's grave " was a great FIICOMSB, as was also ' —though in a less worthy sense by reason of the intrinsic shallowness of the composition—Mr. Coleman's Nazareth." Mr. Crossley conducted with his usual good skill and fine discernment, and Mr. Payton, Mus. Bite., played the pianoforte accompaniments with j itherring judgment and taste.
Ruri-Decanal Conference.

The Rev. Canon Penrhyn presided over the annual conference in connection with the Rand Deanery of 1 Winwick which was held in Toft's 'Assembly Rooms on Thursday evening. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton was re-elected hon. sec. of the conference .Mr. E. Draper being re-elected fion: treasurer. The follow- ing representatives of the Rural Deanery on Diocesan I Commiitees Were appointed :—Finance Association, t Rev. Canon Willis and Captain Withington ; Church Building Society, Rev. J. Carson and Mr. Robert Stone; Benefices Augmentation Fund, Rev. R. Smith and Captain Withinguni ; Standing Committee of Diocesan Conference, Rev. Motley Stevenson, Mr. J. D. Buckton and Mr. R. Stone ; Board of Education, Rev. J. Davies, and Mr. J. D. Buekton ; Church Aid Society, Rev. Canon Penrhyn and Dr. Mouncey.—A long *discussion ensued with regard to the diocesan conference. It was explained that no conference had been held for three years. The hope was expressed that the conference should be held annually.—A vote of thanks to Canon Penrhyn concluded the pro- ceedings. Refreshments were served.

Warrington disappointed their admirers —if there are any left-- by losing at Dewsbury. They were prac- tically at full strength and it must be accounted a very poor performance indeed when the "Cup-holders" fail to beat a last season's second division club. From a Dewsbury point of view the result was very gratify- ing for Warrington were their first --ictims from the select company of the senior division. There was only a point difference ii the scores, but as the homesters scored two tries to IVarrington's one they may fairly lay claim to all the. honours. The War- rington men were a long way below par.

Not long ago Warrington boasted a back division equal to any in the Union' but recently they have fallen upon evil times and it has been the backs who have proved, the stumbling block to the team's pro- gress. First one and then another of the most prominent players has been placed on the injured list and their places been taken by players who have only , partially been successful. For practically the whole ; For to-day's match the Warrington team has been of the season the team has been without the services selected as follows*: Knight full back, Fish, Jones, of Fish and Saturday the crack winger made his Jordan nod Widdeson threequarters ; Hockenhall and re-appearance but what was gained in this respect was Brooks half backs ; Boardman,Preston,Slingars, Jolley, lost by Isherwood not turning out owing to injury. True he occasion- The "A " team will have a stiff combination en- ally gave flashes of that brilliance which is associated gagement at St. Helens and nothing is being left to with his name, but generally speaking his display chance. The following strong side has been chosen to t was exceedingly weak: This comes of playing a man upset the pretentious of the Saints ; Hallam, full before he has got into condition, and as much of the , back ; Turner, Hewitt, Lloyd and Kenyon three- blame devolves upon a majority of the Committee as quarters ; Garside and Davies half backs ; Thomas, ;upon Fish. The remaining backs were an uncertain Lunt, Cook, Forster, and Ashton forwards. quantity, and gave only an average eihibitiou. Jones ' again figured at centre, and what little he had to do he did well, but he was sadly neglected by the halves. This was no fault of Hockenhall's, who prior to his injury to his hand played a sound game, but could be laid at Brooks' door. The " baby " was slow, and his methods lacked that dash and originality necessary in a good half back. Knight at full back was not calculated to inspire confidence. He was slow and shaky, and contributed iu no small degree to the defeat of the team. A word of praise is due to the forwards, who easily held their own. In the scrum /they repeat- edly gained possession, but were a trifita slow in the loose. Had the backs given as good an account of themselves, the match would have had a different end- ing.

Fish has been training this week, and it is hoped that " Jack " will be himself again for the rest of the season. He and Widdeson are sure of a rousing reception at Wilderspool. It will be the latter's first home appearance in the Warrington colours. He is displayin good form week by week, and the pity is that the three-quarter line is weakened by the absence of Isherwood. He has an injured heel, but is expected to be very soon fit again.

more confidence in their own ability than any other team the " All Blacks " have met. They mapped out a spoiling and winning plan of campaign and they canied it to a successful issue. The New Zealanders were played on and "spotted" as they had never been before with the result that they were completely thrown off their balance and lost by a try to nil after having all the worst of the game. The match was a deadly affair, I understand, and our thank.; are due to gallant Wales for proving that the men from the Antipodes are not so super-excellent as to be invincible. What Wales have d me, lam pretty certain the Northent Union could accomplish and it is a matter for increasing regret that the professional body hal no chance of restoring the prestige of Old England against the "All Blacks."

There is a big chance of Warrington's fortunes being revived this holiday week end by a special effort on the part of the players. They have a fair chance of securing six valuable points and I hope they will not let it slip. St. Helens are due at Wilders- pool to-day and though they-had a pretty successful season them should be no doubt as to Warrington's superiority by, the close of play. On Monday, the team goes to Leigh fully determined to wipe out the Lancashire Cup defeat, and seeing how the Mather— lane men shaped on Saturday last the outlook is promising. On Tuesday one of the best matches o the season should be seen at Wilderspuol. Salto are the visitors on that day and with Lomas and hia men in such strong form a battle royal should result.

My Dear Children,— First of all, I muss wish you all a very happy Christmas. Tile same wishes are ex- pressed year after year, but I think it would hardly be like Christmas if friends did not express to one another all good wishes at this season of the year. .

No* for the result of the special competi- tions. Of course, it would be utterly im- possible for me to publish all the contribu- tions that I have received, and this week I have only room for the prize Christmas story. I shall print, later on, selected stories, if I can find space in your columns. The competition for the best story has pro- duced the largest number of replies. No one has sent a very. good account of Santa Claus. Below we print the two best mottoes for 1906. The following have been awarded the prizes in connection with the Christroas competitions:— William Tyler' Elsie Hughes, Margaret M. Press, Annie Kendall, Prudence Musty, Harry W. Smith, William Bury, and Alice Walters. Below I give two very good puzzles, and I shall award two prize volumes to the first correct answers received.
Many thanks to Thomas Thacker for his letter, and the two new names he sent me for the League. I also received a nice letter from Prudence Musty, and shall be glad to receive her as a member.
Well, I must not take up any more space, so I will finish my letter by again wishing you all a very bright and happy time. From UNCLE NED.

woven them together, she wreathed the ture of the Cross. The hanging ivy ,irays veiled its sadness, and the flowers ieemed typical of the purity and perfection "Him who was crucified." The invalid smiled his satisfaction. "That is a fitting wreath for the great symbol," he said, and he lay with his eyes fixed upon it, and his face full of peace. He was unconscious for a while of the physical suffering which was ever present with him. To-night that also was as a veiled Cross. She saw the tired eyes gradually close, watched the weary lines of his face relaxing, and then stole softly out.

There were many small charities over which she must busy herself to-night. She knew he would not be lonely, for his mind was full of beautiful thoughts. Even though driven out at times by physical suffering, they would come back to him like homing birds. Presently he passed into a fairer world than this, the world of dreams. He forgot his .crippled hands; forgot that he was not well and strong as other men. He thought he was once more in his studio, pursuing the art he loved; and the picture upon the easel was a Cross—not such a one as he had painted of old. From the radiated marvellous points of light, which gave it a starlike look; its harsh outlines were soft- ened. It had lost altogether the appear- ance of an instrument of torture. Towards it were hastening men and women, the tired brothers and sisters of the Christ-Child, and in their faces was the' light of hope. He looked at his own picture wistfully. Was there in it all a deeper meaning than he (the artist) could fathom? Had he painted greater than he knew? Suddenly the \ room filled with radiance. A little Child was standing beside him, the Child to whom we turn at Yuletide, bringing other gifts than did the Wise Men, yet perhaps as welcome in the eyes of Him with whom we have to do. He pointed tt? the Cross in the picture, and the man whose genius had wrought it trembled exceedingly. "Though art the Christ-Child," he cried. "Though art He who, as each Christmas- tide comes round, doth draw with invisible cords the hearts of men and women to the faith taught them at their mother's knee; before whose mighty ehild-influence they be- come again as little children. Tell me, is it well that at this season, we, worshipping at Thy cradle, forget for a while the bitter- ness of Thy Cross?" TEC Child's eyes gazed upon the picture, and as He gazed, the glory which radiated from it grew more and more dazzling. The form of the Croqs had entirely disappeared in the light which surrounded it. He bowed His head in answer, and the sick man awoke, to find his gaze resting on a picture which was wreathed with' ivy and white roses—" A Veiled Cross."
WILLIAM TYLER

PRIZE CHRISTMAS STORY. THE VEILED CROSS.
A STORY OF YULE,

_ It was Christmas Eve—noi an " old- fashioned " Christmas, but one of • fog and damp. All day long a heavy rain had been falling, but • towards evening its force had abated, and busy folk, on marketing intent, sallied forth into the brightly-lit streets. The wealth of luxuries and solid comforts displayed in the various shop windows seemed boundless. Despite the untoward weather, friends and neighbours found them- selves exchangirig cheerful greetings as•" of old, and wishing each other, as in times gone by, "A Merry Christmas." In a large old-fashioned house, which stood in a quiet square, busy hands were ,employed in decorating every available spot with holly and evergreens. The dining-room, usually a somewhat gloomy apartment, panelled in oak, and furnished in the fashion of a bY- gone century, had been completely trans- formed. Behind the tarnished guilt frames which held the portraits of dead ilnd gone ancestors, gleamed great clusters bf scarlet berries and shining leaves, arranged by the instinct of an artist. It was a woman whose -clever fingers had wrought the magical trans- forming touches, and as ,she looked ,around her with keen satisfaction, as She stood in the middle of the dusky room, the firelight played on her sweet expressive face: , It is beautiful," she said. " I have done it myself, but I do really think it is beau- tiful." She turned lovingly to someone who was lying on a couch which had been drawn near the fire. An invalid lay there, a man on whose face pain had drawn many weary lines. He answered her with a kindly ex- pression in his hollow eyes, saying, " my daughter, it is. beautiful, but you have left one picture untouched. Is not the Cross also to share in the beauty of Christmas ? " He indicated a picture which he himself had painted before the illness came which had crippled his gifted fingers. It was a solitary cross standing on a hillside in the faint light of dawn. Its upper beams were touched with golden glory. They stood sharply out against a background of lower- ing clouds, symbolical and majestic. The sick man's gaze lingered tenderly on the picture: It was the last he had painted ere his brilliant career was cut short, and it had ever since been to him a comfort and inspiration. "You have left the Cross untouched," he 'repeated. " Why ? " She drew 'nearer by his compelling gaze. and half whispered, "It is the time of the Nativity, I know, but would it be reverent to hide the Cross?" ." No," be answered. "The Cross cannot be hidden, for it is always with us—with us, beloved, in a suffering world; in the broken hearts of our brothers and sisters. But at the blessed season of Yule we may veil the Cross of Calvary, and remember only the cradle of Bethlehem. We can forget our individual sorrows, and join heartily in the great world of happiness. It is right that it should be so." She went to the table, and took therefrom some delicate sprays of ivy and Christmas roses, white as undriven snow. When she
