WARRINGTON AGRICULTURAL I SOCIETY. .
Annual Meeting.
PROPOSED EXTENDED RADIUS.

The annual meeting in connection with the Warring- ton and District Agricultural Society was held at the Masonic Hell, Bold-street. on Tuesday, Sir Gilbert Greenell, Baru presiding ovor a 1 trg.e attendance. / ANNUAL, REPOIcrs.

'I he staten); et I.r accounts Sll:lthitted by the Tressu Cr Mr. Alfred Broome. showed that ou the year's woreine there was a loss £llB Ills. sd. Sir Gilbert Greene!' had however'made a speciel donation to the funds of . £lOO and this together with a credit balance on the ' previous year left the Society with a balance in hand if £24 15s. 2d. Mr. H. BELESFORD MELVILLE submitted his report, in which he said it only required a casual glance to realise that a great step bed been taken in the work I done by the Society. The catalogue for the last show showed an increase of entries, and increased interest was shown throughout. There was a slight falling oft in numbers of shire entries and draught geldings, but the judges expiessed themss Ives entirely satisfied with the quality, and in some cases there appeated diffi- culty to say to which exhibits the prizes should go. There were two entries in the yearling, two-year-old, and three-year-old classes. The hunters and harness classes far surpassed anything ever shown at Walton or possibly at any show of the year, both for quantity and quality. 'I he addition of novice classes was art entirely new depsrture, and the resuit gave evidence of the appreciation of such classes. The tradesmen's and tenant furtuer's turn-out classes were not a success' excepting for light horses (single or pair). Every entry in the class for a team of hoist a was specially asked for, and was sent as a favour mole to till up the class than to win pr. sett. It is thought that this class in future might easily I e ithciramn, as there apparently is little or no femme( it ion in teams. There was a good show in eutt te atm pigs, rem a t try fair one in cheese. The entries of butter were poor, and although there was a slight alteration in the offer of the prizes there seems to be very little interest taken in the class. A great number of new members have joined the Society, but there still requires more support to make the Society self-suppotting. A guarantee fund is not altogether desirable, but the time l has come when the Society should be placed on a firmer footing, and the Council are quite prepared to consider any scheme likely to ensure such a result. By the kind assistance of Lady Greene!' it is intended to hold a flower and vegetable show in Walton Park on the day of this Seciety's show next year, when prizes I will be offered to residents in the parish of Walton andi to the estate workpeople employed by Sir Gilbert ! Oreenall. Lady rt smell Las offered, for the first year, to provide the m hole or the prizes". The Secretary to the Warrington Shire Horse Society has reported the follom lug t,Der by Meisrs. Aiuscotigh, Buiscutigh Mills, Ormskirk. Messrs. Ainsco nth will give four special premiums of 7 guineas each for the four best slAre brood wares stinted to " Ambush " in season 1006 and proved to be in foal, such prizes to be judged for in special classes at the Warrington Agricultural show in 1906. Messrs. Ainscough will also offer special foal premiums got by the same horse. The question of the extension of the district is a matter which ought now to be seriously considered, as the 12 mile radius round Warrington does not extend I sufficiently into the cheese, butter and hunter districts of Cheshire. It is therefore proposed to increase the I size of the radius to 10 miles in Cheshire, except that part of Cheshire lying east of the railway from Broad- heath to Manchester, and north of the railway from Broadbent)] to Stockport. _ _ .

The CHAIRMAN Sard it was desirable that the mem- bership of the Society should be increased. The ques- tion of the alteration of the radius of the Society required careful consideration Last veer they had to refuse a large number of entries which were just out- side the district.
The reports were approved on the motion of Mr.R.B. Neilson, seconded by :dr. C. E. Liraker, jun.

div.head: SUGGESTED- ALTERATION OF THE RADIUS.
div.p: SUGGESTED- ALTERATION OF THE RADIUS.

The following proposed alteration in the rules was submitted to the meeting for consideration : "The district of the Society consists of such portion of Lan- cashire as lies within a radius cf I'2 miles of Market. gate, Warrington, and of such portion of Cheshire as lies within 16 miles of the same point, save and except that part of Cheshire lying East of the 'Amoy from 13roadheath to IManchester end North of the railway from Broadheath to Stockport is excluded. The farm house and buildings of an exhibitor in the district classes must be situate within the district, and all exhibitors (except for open and special classes, if any) must reside within the Society's district." Mr. S. DAVIES said that they in Cheshire felt that they were not quite satisfied respecting the proposed alteration. It would open core a very wide district and be did not see why it should not be extended to 16 miles all round.' Thelerc instAN : In that eventwe would clash with many local societies. Mr. 0. R. NEWTON asked why a certain portion of the radius should be excluded. Be personally preferred I that there should be no alteration at all, as he did not think the proposal would be of any benefit to the show either in respect to au increase in membership or financially. Mr. T.Ssirrit said that if the radius were increased one or two cattle breecleis would be admitted who would sweep the board and carry off all the prizes. On a vote being taken it was decided by a largo majority to make no alteration in the radius and the motion was lost.
A vote of thanks to Sir Gilbert Greenall for presid- ing concluded the meeting.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 23, 1905.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
CORRESPONDENTS are particularly requested to send letters intended for Friday's " Examiner " not later than Thursday morning. _ MR. A. H. CROSFIELD REPLIES TO MR. F. MONKS.
The Home Rule and Free Trade Questions.

Sir,—The following letter from Mr. F. Monks appeared in your paper last week. I have divided it into paragraphs for the sake of convenience in referring to the topics Mr. Monks raises. A.—Dear sir, I know there are many voters who would be glad of a definite pronouncement by the two candidates for Parliamentary representation at the forthcoming election, upon the following : Home Rule for Ireland in view of the appointment of two such avowed Houle Rulers as Lord Aberdeen and Mr. Bryce. B.—For Free Trade, both Imports and Exports as between different nations I take it there is no diver- gence of opinion,but the free importation of products from countries that protect their own industries to the exclusion of our own, is one-side and works to the disadvantage of many of our owff industries. C.—Do the candidates favour a Revision of our Tariff Laws for revenue only, or do they favour such alteration in the Tariff Laws as shall lead to Prefer- ential Trading with those countries who admit our productions upon an equitable basis and contribute to our Imperial taxation. D.—Do they favour a Redistribution Bill which shall give a fair representation in proportion to population and taxation.—Yours faithfully, (Signed) F. Mos Ks. A.—lf Mr. Monks means : Am I in favour of the next Libaral Government creating a subordinate Parlia- ment in Dub!in with an Executive responsible to it, No, lam not. Before reading Mr. Monks' questions I had already stated publicly and privately that, allied as we are with many Unionists and Conservatives in defence of Free Trade, there must be some give and take on this question. What will be its ultimate solu- tion in the future Ido not pretend to prophesy. Home Rule all round may have to be considered, and such schemes as Sir Charles Dilke has lately put forward ; or in relieving a congested Parliament, notoriously overloaded with work, it may be better to deal with Ireland first. But although I will not take it upon myself to prophesy as to the future, I have no hesitation in telling Mr. Monks what I think should be the guiding prin- ciple for Liberals in the next Parliament, which by the way, it is evidently admitted by men of all parties is going to be a Liberal Parliament. That guiding i prin- ciple was admirably expressed by Mr. Haldane n the brilliant speech he made towards the close of last month at Frodsham. This is what he said : "The first thing the people of this country should do if the Liberals came into power was to insist that the government of Ireland should, in Lincoln's favourite phrase, be for the peeple,th rough the people and by the people. If they could not do that directly they could do it indirectly. Sixty years ago the Whig Prime Minister was -Lord Melbourne, and he sent to Ireland as his Under Secre- tary a young engineer of genius named Thomas Drummond. He managed Irish affairs for several years, and he killed himself with overwork, but Thomas Drummond left a memory which showed that with sympathetic administration the whole aspect of affairs at Dublin Castle could be changed, and what Thomas Drummond tried to do, it was the duty of the Liberal party to enable Sir Antony Mac Donnell to do in reality, and thereby educate not only the people of Ireland themselves in the way in which they might attain their goal, and in the end govern their own concerns through the medium of their own repro. sentatives sitting in Ireland, and relieving the Imperial Parliament of a duty it was ill-adapted to discharge." Having answered Mr. Monks' first question, perhaps he will allow me to ask him one or two questions on the same subject. Jest a week ago, after Lord Dudley had laid down his office of Viceroy, during a period in which he and Lady Dudley have earned a good deal of respect and affection in Ireland, the " Times " news- paper, after alluding to Lord Dudley's genial manner and love of sport, and Lady Dudley's keen and sym- pathetic interest in Irish affairs, continues after this preamble to say that "All these considerations make Irish Unionists anxious as far as possible to overlook Lord Dudley's unhappy association with political intrigue"; and adds that there "can be little doubt that his comparative ignorance of Irish politics and his great desire to be popular with the mass of the people were contributing causes to the events -that brought about Mr. Wyndha.m's fall." We are to gather that Lord Dudley fell, though he did not resign, from the same cause, because "he had a habit of letting his sympathies run away with him," of which the evidence is that some of his speeches in Ireland, " aotably the one in whioh he talked about 'governing Ireland acoording te Irish ideas' did much misehief." As the" Westminster Gazette" remarks,"we must be really gratefal to any one who illustrates so perfectly what may be called the temper of the Ascendency Party." The same issue of the "Times "contains one of Sir Henry Howerth's letters from the Carlten Club. In passing, this outspoken Conservative, after referring to Mr. Balfour as our "Incomparable Steersman "says that the personnel of the new Cabinet is at least as good as its predecessor—"it does not for instance contain examples of the notorious nonentities who have been its greatest source of weakness to the late Tory Government." Butlhe portion of his letter to which I would pdrticulary draw Mr. Monks' attention, is the following. Sir Henry lloworth is evidently alarmed at the indifference the constituencies show to the Irish bogey,which our Conservative friends in their desperate straits are drawing out. He fears this cry will serve the Unionist party at the polls no better than Mr. Balfour's throwing up the sponge has done as a pre- liminary move, and by way of explaining his depression at the situation he writes :

- "As if to make the position completely topsy turvy, the official champions of the Union. for which we have fought so long and sacrificed so much, could not apparently find among their loyal servants men they deem competent to immediately control and direct the great machine of the Executive in Ireland, and must perforce send to India for two avowed Home Rulers, tied by the closest ties to the Irish Priest- hood. and the Nationalist leaders, Sir A. Mac Donnell and Mr. Finucane, and put them in charge of the steering apparatus itself. Now we have the grotesque situation perfectly obvious to the man in the street, that the Liberals, to whom we hauled down our flag so gaily a fortnight ago, actually find ready to their hands two heads of the Executive is Ireland, whose antecedents and whose connections make them the most suitable instruments they could find all the world over for carrying out the policy of sap and mine which they have determined upon. They are saying, quite truly,that all they mean to do is to give a free hand to the two Irish officials Who were ap- pointed and patronised by the Unionists and left in office when they resigned." If Sir Henry in ttikiwr about " stp?ing and mining" means that the English Liberals are directly or indirectly going to support a policy that will lead up to an independent Parliament, of course I utterly dis- agree with him. But what about this appointment of Sir A. Mac Donnell and Mr. Finucane in 1902 ; the , appointment made by Mr. Wyndham and approved by I Mr. Balfour. Does Mr. Monks condemn the appoint- ment of those men and their work as welt? Does he condemn the appointment of Lord Dudley and Mr Wyndham, and their policy of " Governing Ireland according to Irish ideas ?" I am quite sure there are many voters who would be glad to know Mr. Monks' answer, and to hear what Mr. Pierpoint has to say. Did he view theseappointments and their consequences with the same apprehension as the appointment of Lord Aberdeen and Mr. Bryce. The opinion of that most Ultra-Tory group in the United Kingdom, the party of ascendency in Belfast, we know quite well because it was expressed quite frankly in the House of Commons by one of their number (I just forget his name, and have no means of reference here) ; but what he said, referring to the policy of Lord Dudley and Mr. Wynd- ham was that "while a policy of conciliation was all right in theory, it was sickening in practice." Do Mr. Monks and Mr. Pierpoint agree ? I am informed Mr. Monks still professes sympathy with Liberal ideas. I know that he did so a very few years since. It would be a matter of very great regret to many friends of his in Warringion, who esteem and honour him, to hear that he had become more Tory than the Tories. 11.—I disagree with Mr. Monks. Free Trade all round would of course be far better than the present system, but" Half a loaf is better than no bread." The great controversy of the last two years has proved to the hilt, that as Mr. Asquith says, " Whatever may be , the case with other people, cheap food and cheap raw , material and the open market are with us here in this country the life blood of our industries." .

C.—There is not a little Balfourian vaguenesss at)out this. I do not know whether the question means, " Do you support Balfour's policy, or Chamberlain's, or bah ?" My answer is, Neither. I do not think I need in turn ask Mr. Monks which policy he supports, because I am afraid we all know quite well, that he and Mr. J. J. Bleckley and Mr. W. P. Rylands have been caught by Joe's 10 per cent, bait, and the prospect of profitable little combinations at other people's expense behind this protective barrier. The wonder to me is that after his long Liberal career in the past Mr. F. Monks can shut his eyes to the other side of the question. I have argued it out in detail more than once, and it is only necessary at this time of day to briefly point out that the Agricultural interest would not be satisfied with a 2s. a quarter duty on wheat, or a 5 per cent, duty on foreign pleat (excepting bacon, eggs, butter and ileese). Experience abroad has shown us the tendency of these corn duties to rise rapidly,and how the increased cost of everything reduces the purchasing power of the wages of the great mass of the people. It also shows us that as an inevitable con- sequence of this reduced spending power, when the first

necessaries of life have been satisfied, there is less money with which to purchase other articles. The overwhelm- ing importance of the home market. and the fatal conse- quences of reducing demand there must be patent to anyone who thinks for half a minute on the matter, and I am happy to know that the ironworkers at any rate are as fully alive to them as their leaders, and indeed all the powerful Labour leaders to a man throughout the country. As facts are stronger than arguments. here are a few from Germany that absolutely prove our contention :- 1 "The reports of the Chambers of Commerce teem with suggestive facts showing the close connection between high prices of food and commercial depression in the home trade and establishing beyond doubt that it is this which supplies the explanation of ; the complaints of depression arising from o rev-produc- tion or rather under-consuruptton n many industries. We have a striking picture of the effects of the higher foodlprices on a great retell trade, viz., hoots and shoes. As recently as 1902 "Der Arbeitsmarkt" wrote of the great dissatisfaction felt at the result of the year's turnover, which showed "a rapid decline in the consumption of shoes." Men and women (continued the report), who in the ordinary way have two ptirs of boots in use and are accustomed to buy one new pair every year have this year in many cases Wen unable to purchase any. Moreover people are more careful in the wear of their boots, and, content themselves with repairs where in former years a flea' pair would have be.m obtained. So far as new new purchases are made, the buyers demand cheaper qualities than formerly ; every other branch of the clothing trades could tell the same depressing tale. Each fresh turn of the Protection screw, every new regulation to restrict the importation of grain and live stock across . .

the frontiers, has forthwith-a re-action in the form of reduced purchases of articles of attire." Is it necessary to point out that reduced consumption means slack production with its inevitable consequences on employment and wages: what then are we to think of these promises of more employment? This is wait Lord Hugh Cecil has to say "Mr. Chamberlain told them his policy would mean more work at home and the union of the Empire. Nothing could be nicer. The argument of stagnant export trade has been superseded by that of unem- ployment. The question of the unemployed was a very sad one, but to take advantage of the distress of poor people and-to tell them of one bad remedy which was no remedy, and to put before them the hope of amelioration by a change of policy which if it affected them at all, would make them worse Oil than to-day --was a thing against which they ought to protest with all their power." But have I misunderstood my old and respected . friend Mr. Monks ? Is he in the dry light of facts in- clined to whittle dawn .qr. mnberlitin's general 10 per cent. tariff, and will he rather fight under Mr. Balfour's flag ? And lam sure a great many people in Warrington will be much interested to know whether Mr. Pierpoint intends to follow Mr.Btlfour,or whether he sticks to the Chamberlain colours and to the policy which he and Colonel Howard Vincent—that energetic High Priest of Protection—have vigorously preached to ,1 us in Warrington. If the line is to be drawn now at Mr. I Balfour's policy,isn't it about time we knew exactlywhere 'he stands, because after his subtle and ingenious speech at Manchester, the next morning as usual half a dozen Conservative papers were interpreting it in as many different ways. No wonder that the humorous and ever outspoken Member for Bolton suggests that If Mr. Balfour wants a crest he might adopt that of the Isle of Man—three legs rruming round and round. so that you don't know which the thing stands on." But if anyone is seriously attracted by the policy of Prefer- ence, I would strongly recommend him, or her. to read L. G. C. Money's pamphlet "Through Preference to Protection," because I venture to say nothing abler or more concln sive has ever been published on the subject. D.—We Liberals shall be perfectly ready to discuss this question when the time is ripe for it it is not ripe yet. Mr. Asquith in the speech from which I have al- ready quoted, after referring to the extraordinary per- formances of the late Government, and pointing out that they are trying to run away from the issue that they themselves have raised, says :—" For what is the latest phase in this protracted game of alternate bluff and defiance ? It is to attempt to steal votes for Pro- tection under the cover of an artificial outcry about Home Rule." I am afraid the redistribution proposal was made with not very dissimilar motives, and r regret that Mr. Monks can lend his name to such pitiful party tactics.—Yours etc., Dec. 21st.
A. H. CROSFIELD.

div.head: Cost of the Sugar Convention.
div.p: The Cost of the Sugar Convention.

Sir,—Your correspondent 1117. J. Gandy referring to sugar states that although the bounties are abolished sugar is again wonderfully cheap. Now that a fair time has elapsed since the Brussels Sugar Convention came into force, it is worth while to gauge the conse- quences of the action of the late Government in making England a party to this. It may be well to state the objects which induced our late rulers to enter into this Convention. The principal object was to prevent sugar coming into this country which had been artificially cheapened by foreign bounties (averaging about a half- penny per pound) in order that the sugar cane industry in the West Indies might get the better price of this produce. The secondary objects were to widen the area of cultivation, espesially in the Pinapirs, to make prices steady and to establish the selling prices of sugar on a natural basis.

Taking the secondary objects first. Instead of making prices steady we have had the most violent fluctuations, beet sugar (SS per cent.) having fluctuated between Os. to 16.0 F. 0.8. Defenders of the Convention seek to attribute this variation to the effect of the drought of 1904. In this they are in part justified. We all know that the value of a necessary like sugar must be affected by the crop, although the shortage in this case was grossly exaggerated. Where they err is in shutting their eyes to the influence of the Convention in creating conditions which have more than doubled the price of sugar. The drought was responsible for a shortage in the European output of 20 per cent, on the previous year. There never was a real shortage, but by limiting, our freedom of purchase to particular countries, and those most affected by the drought, we lessened the markets from which we could buy. This gave the opportunity for speculators,led byMr. Cronier,r to corner the visible supplies in the restricted con- vention area. They knew well that England had tied her hands and could not purchase in the world's market, be- cause of the boycott convention terms. They recognized (that which English Convention defenders have been slow to acknowledge) that the cheap sugar available for Englitnd would stimulate the consumption for private and industrial purposes on the Continent. The specu- lators played the game boldly, sugar was held off the market and prices forced up the corner lasted longer than any previous one in this article. But the bulls held on too long, nature was bountiful and promised a bumper crop, the bears came out and had a rollicking time, The weak holders gave way and bolted, the strongest came a cropper and committed suicide, and sugar came down with a rush. The convention there- fore which was destined to "steady prices "has helped to cause the most violent fluctuations, and instead of getting it at its "natural price " we have helped to make it an easy prey for the speculator. Such violent oscillation in price give little cause for confidence to the East India planters, and this was one of the objects of the convention. Turning to the question of the expected increase of sugar production in the Empire, especially in the West Indies, we find according to Willettand Gray's estimate the following figures : Sugar crop of West Indies.

1991-2 .. 165,000 tons. 1902-3 ... 117,630 tons. 1903-1 ... 135,364 tons. 1904-5 ... 102,000 tons. Thus we see in spite of our sacriflce in paying about £5,000,000 per annum more for our sugar we have not been able to stimulate this declining industry, we have tied our hands, and that for another three years, by a clumsy arrangement whereby our Continental rivals get all the benefit and we all the loss.

In view of the above facts and figures it is amusing to read the recent utterance of Mr. It. Pierpoint, M.P., who damns the Convention by faint praise in the following words :—" They could remembe not very long ago in that room he had made some remarks about the Sugar Convention. All talk about it had now practically ceased because unfortunately for the prophecies sugar WnS down at its normal price. It was unfortunate to find when they had been saying dis- agreeable things about a particular Convention that after all it had done no harm but perhaps a great deal of good in our Colonies."

The effect upon our home consumption may be gathered from the following figures : Import of Sugar into Great Britain September to August in the followinz years. Av'gecost Quantity Value per cwt. cwt. R. s. d. 1901-9 34,631,125 ... 16,782,410 ... 9 S 1902 9 30,955,119 ... 14,898,895 ... 9 -8 1903-4 3O 931 868 ... 15 971.699 ... 10 4 . .. .. ..

1904-5 Reckoning the 1904-5 import at the 1901-2 price, we find that we have paid six and a half millions more for our sugar, whereas if our imports had not been checked by high prices and we had maintained our import on the 1901-2 level we should have paid eight millions more. This increased cost is largely due to the short crop, which was taken advantage of by speculators cornering the supply—this made easy by our own foolish act—but it is also largely due to the abolition of the bounties, which while reducing our supply of cheap sugar has stimulated the Continental consumption, which has enormously increased. CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, December 20th, 1905.

div.head: --- Liberal Inconsistencies.
div.p: --- Liberal Inconsistencies.

Sir,—The letter from Hr. Gandy's pen on this theme in your last issue was so plausible that I feel some answer will bo looked for from those who personally or as partisans are involved in his condemnation. In the first place I should like to thank Mr. Gaudy for the public service he has rendered by urging on politiciar a high level of charity, and civility. The moment

could not be more opportune for pointing out that, if I we are to be gentlemen,the same rules are effective for I forensic purposes as are enforced by our social code for domestic discussion. I have been particularly pained by the persistent malignity with which during the last few years the personal motives have been canvassed of one particular man. I au not for a moment going to draw any analogy between the two men, but most of us may recall that the late Mr. Gladstone was the object of similar virulent attacks from a certain class of mediocrities. Surely it punt he clear to any thinking person that nothing is gained by such ungentlemauliness. On the contrary it provokes resentment and stiffens apposition into absolute obstinacy, making all discussion futile, where a more charitable and concessive attitude would open the way to con- viction. Nothing would, I maintain, be lost in the conflict by recognising Mr. Caarnberlain's pre-eminent ability and his past services to the state. I hope my Liberal comrades •in this fight—for in this question, though nat in all, lam on the Liberal side—will not take it amiss if I plead with them to set in this Free Trade campaign a high example of civility and to abstain from personalities which only prejudice the question. Approaching now the corpus of Nlr. Gandy's letter ; he asks us whether we really and truly believe in the principles we profess. Speaking for myself as well as for my colleagues, I say we do. He cites the associa- iation we have formed for mutual protection. We hive ' he says. from time the time bound ourselves not to sell certain classes of goals (" foods " is no doubt a mis- print) under fixed prices. It is true we have so bound ourselves nat natuiler pse %Wes. The agreement is a matter of honour only, hot that point is quite immaterial. The material point is :—What is the effect of the agreement! How fa' does it imp Lir freederu Of trade? Some of us remember well the coal miners' strike of 1833. I believe I am right in saying that the great bulk of their countrymen were in complete sym- pathy with the men in that dispute. And why? because it was then brought home as never before that competition is not always for the public good. The principle came then to be accepted that employers may not compete with one another and force down prices without considering the demands for a living wage. But in our trade unrestrained competition may do other ruischi4f. Firms may compete not merely by forcing down the wages of their employe, but by reducing the quality of their goods, and it is against this latter danger that we secure ourselves, for while by these agreements we are bound as to price, we are not bound as to quantity or quality. We have simply eliminated the two factors which work to the public dis- advantage and compete solely on Tiality. Tne result is that in all our products the quality has vastly improved daring the last few years. Take glycerine for example. The stuff we sold some years ago for dynamite glycerine would not be marketable to-day for that purpose. What was accepted 10 years ago as chemically pure glycerine would not pass for pure to-day. As a consequence the English chemically pure glycerine has invaded Germany and absolutely routed the German commodity on its own protected field. Thus it, must be clear to any unprejudiced person that the agreements Mr. Gandy mentions far from impairing freedom of trade, confine that freedom within healthy limite which make for the advantage not only of the manufacturers and the men, but above all for the consumer, whose greatest interest is in the purity of the product. The same tale could no doubt be told for seme other manufacturers. My only purpose at p.aesent is to vindicate my own motives and those of my friends and to show that it is not against the evils of Free Trade that we have taken measures to protect ourselves but against that deterioration in the product which is the result of indiscriminate competition. As for fiscal protection my experience-is as I have said before that it is only required by those manufacturers who are behind the times. These snatikh at the fiscal straw because they do not see that the true and only remedy is education, physical, mental, and moral. Unless we recegnise this we shall lose the only advantage to be gained by the present controversy. I insist that the education should be complete and complete it cannot be in my opinion and in the opinion of many others with- out a system of national training. Indeed so strong is this conviction with rue that were two men to present themselves one of whom were to declare himself favour- able to this policy, the other not, I should feel com- pelled to record my vote for the former without regard to his attitude on the fiscal question.—l am yours &c. K. a MARKEL. Tower House, Bewsey, 20th December, 1905. - _ Small-Pox at Stockton Heath.

Sir,-31y attention having been directed to the report of Dr. Adams at the recent meeting of the Runcorn District Council, as reported in your paper, I regret to have to say that it is both inaccurate and misle tding so far :.s it relates to my intercourse with him. I should be justified in usincr very strong epithets in relation to the matter, but will content myself with the following observations :-Ist. Dr. Adams did not at any time suggest, or in any way intimate, that I could call in my own doctor, nor did he ever mention the matter until I had taken action. 2nd. I have not written six letters to Dr. Adams. and, in those I have written, I have neither used abusive language, or imputed base motives to him, but when my efforts to get my own doctor to see my son failed I did severely criticize his atbitude. 3rd. As to Mr. Whitley's remarks—they are highly characteristic of the man, but he is entirely mistaken. For obvious veasoas I have observed a strut reticence, bat when questioned I have ventured to express an opinion for which I believe I have the best of reasons,an opinion which I have held from the first and still hold. To those who are so dense that they cannot distinguish between the expression of opinion and positive assertion.it is useless to appeal. Yours, s; MOSS.

div.head: LIBRARY.
div.p: THE LIBRARY.
Unveiling of a Memorial Tablet.
The Early History of the Institution.

IWarrington boasts the distinction of possessing the first rate-supported Free Library established in this country. The institution dates back, as a Corporation undertaking to November 19th, 1813, and the present building which servos as a :lluseum, Library and Art Gallery, was opened in 1857. It is fitting that the out- standing points in the history of such an old and useful institution should be promin- ently placed on record and with this object in view, a memorial inscription which has been engraved on brass in the entrance hall was unveiled on Tuesday afternoon by Alderman Bennett (chairman of the Museum Committee). The tablet is a handsome piece of work and the words inscribed upon it are as follows: ' —County Borough of Warrington. The Municipal Museum, containing the first rate-supported Free Library, established in this country, was opened to the public Ist November. 1818, and was placed in this building in the year 1857. There was a large attendance to witness the interest- ing ceremony. The guests assembled in the Art gallery where refreshments were served and opportunity was also taken to inspect several recent additions to the collections. Afterwards an adjournment was made to the entrance hall. Before unveiling the tablet Alderman TlctixETT delivered an interesting address on the early history of the Library. He said the library was actually formed on May Ist. 1760. At this particular period there were probably not half a dozen libraries in Lancashire and Cheshire—he only knew of four the Chetham Library at Manchester. which dated from 1653 : the Cheshire Library at Halton,which dated from 1732; the Shepherd Library at Preston, which dated from 1759—a1l free foundations, and the Liverpool (Lyceum) Library, established, like the Warrington one, upon a proprietary basis. just two years earlier, that was to say, in 1754. In 1845 an Act was passed empowering boroughs with a population of 10,090 to build museums, and to raise a halfpenny rate for their support, and in 1817, " the ;good old town" was incorporated, with Mr. William Beamont as its earliest mayor, and John Fitchett Marsh as its first town clerk. The Town Council had not been in power a year when Mr. Fitchett Marsh drew up proposals for the establish- merit or a" Warrington Museum and library, under the ; 8 and 9 Vic. c. 43,by merging therewith the Warrington Town Library and the Museum of the Natural History Society."—Two places only, Canterbury and Leicester, had availed themselves, as yet, of the advantages con- ceded by the Act, and founded in their midst their own museums, and it was left for Warrington to couple with the scheme a ,locril library, and so to win the great dis- tinction which they celebrated that day, the right they claimed to be regarded as the first free rate-supported Library in England. Surely that was someting to be proud of ! Surely it was something to which, in this money-grubbing age, they might look back with pleasure and recall with pride ! The tablet having been unveiled, Mr. J. C. RIDGWAY (deputy chairman of the committee) delivered a short address on the growth of the Library and Mr. L. GREENING dealt in an interesting Yray• with the history of the Museum which had its beginnings in 1835 when the Natural History Society formed a collection.

div.head: Fatal Scratch.
div.p: A Fatal Scratch.

A Warrington jury on Thursday returned a verdict of accidental death at an inquest on Sarah Ellen Murphy,44,wife of a lal3ourer,residing in Tilley-street. On December 20th, Mrs. Murphy was going about the kitchen doing workhouse when she caught her leg against a small wooden stool.A. week later she had to be removed to the infirmary, where she was attended to for a small ulcer on the leg. Erysipelas set in, and death followed on Monday.

div.head: HAPPINESS OR MISERY.
div.p: HAPPINESS OR MISERY.
POLITICAL IMPRESSIONS
(Continue,/ From. L2st Week.)
a The historical que3tion, Who dia it ? and the financial question, Who paici for it ? were both settled before the new lamp was lighted the nest evening."—Oliver Wendell Holmes. 1899.

Now let us consider, for a m.ornent, wnut r learned friend has stated. You will remember that in the quotation from sir. Hughes' pamphlet which I gave last week there was the following sentence : " When the future historian of our EmPiresomes to examine into this Chinese labour episolle, he may pat forward a theory which would perhaps startle our Liberal friends of to-day, if they could come back to read the unwelcome verdict which posterity may possibly pass upon much that was done and left undone in South Africa, in the early __summer of 1893."
Inly pass an unwelcome verdict—and, of course, he mar ra,t. The writer of the articles thinks that he will. I think that he will not. And I will tell you why.

Mr. Hughes thinks—or did think—that if the Liberal party in June 1893—then in Opposition, —had allowed the Government to send out an expeditionary force of 10,009 men td South Africa, perlt ips the whole course pf South African events might have been altered. Now, I consider that statement, in face of what Lord Lansdowne said in the House of Lorl4, and which was reported in the " Minchester Guardian " of 16th Uarch, 1901, to be what is called on the other side of the Atlantic, " buncombe." Really, it is amazing how easily some people are persuaded to put pen to piper. Lord Lansdowne said : We believed that the country was not ready for war in the months of June and July, 189 D, and, we therefore contented ourselves with taking those measures we were advised were suffi.cient to ensure the safety of the Colonies.'

Mind! those are the words of Lord Lansdowne—the Only Lord Lansdowne—who was supposed, at that time, to know everything. Whet has Mr. Hughes to say of "the unwelcome verdict which posterity may possibly pass" if the future historian places that startling sentence in the SohoOlboy's History Book? I wonder whether he has ever read the War gem- mission Report ?

div.head: 1899 IMPERIALISM.
div.p: 1899 IMPERIALISM.

Mr. Hughes has been graciously pleased to refer to the "Daily Mail :" "This new paper (" Daily Mail" did not create Imperialism, it simply voiced it —as no other paper had ever done —for the masses." Now let us see what the " Daily Mail " " voiced " in the year 1899—the 6th October. "It is melancholy to reflect that this hour of I danger to British interests in South Africa is large- ly due to the blindness of General Butler." "Next to President Kruger and the Little England- ers who have egged him on to his defiance of. Britain, Sir W. Butler has been the CallS3 of the present war." Surely, that is not "voicing " Imperialism" for the masses.". Fancy, the Little Englanders egging President Kruger on to defy Great Britain. The population of Great Britain and her ealonies was as 256 to 1 against the Boers. Their chances of beat- ing us were therefore hopeless. Sir W. Butler, as we now know, was appainted to the Aldershot command and his reputation vindicated by that appointment. Lord Wolseley once described him as "the ablest general in the British Army." "It is satisfactory to find," said 'The Star ', 11th Sptetni-yer 19'Y), " that the virulence and the violence of the Yellow Press have not prevailed against the brilliant record of this dis- tinguished soldier." So much; for the" new paper." Mr. flugliss has stated —or inferred—that the Liberals were the cause of the war. The " Daily Mail," Hr. Hughes' imperialist paper, has stated that "next to President Kruger and the Little Englanders, Sir W. Butler has, been the cause of the present war." Lord Lansdowne—Earl Percy's idol —" believed that the country was not ready for the war." I wonder whether, Hr. Hughes has ever read of the Jameson Raid? I should like to remind him of what happened on that glorious land-grabbino. expedition. Perhaps I will some day. It may help him " not to format " a few things. Tfle LABOUR QUESTION.

Let us now turn our attention to the Labour ques- tion in Smith Africa. lam sorry that my friend, Hr. Hughes, speaks so falteringly upon the subject. He is so uncertain, somehow, of his ground. He, surely, does not mean to tell us that the Liberal Party was responsible for the introductien of Chiltese Labour into the Colony. Dart Grey, in addressing the Chartered Company's Shareholders, reported in " The Times " December Dith,_lB99, said

"We dismiss frOrn our minds any idea of develop- ing our mines with white labour. . . . It is obvious that the black labour of the aboriginal inhabitants of South Africa must be our first line of defence. . . . I may add that the directors are already making inquiries on their own account as to the possibility of obtaining 'Asiatic' labour." The star, January 1, 1901 : The other day Mr. Rhodes and his entourage indignantly repudiated any intention to introduce Chinese Labour into Rhodesia. At the time, we received these denials with scepticism. Our atti- tude is amply justified by the report of the Rhodesia Exploration and Development Company, Limited. In the Engineer's annual report we find some very suggestive remarks under the heading " Native Labour." We fear the gentleman" doth protest too much.' His real views leak out in this significant para- graph : I think the introduction of Chinese would be pre- ferableto the introduction of coolies from the min- ing districts of India, for the reason that whereas we could legislate for the Oiliness and treat them as aliens, we could not do so in the case of Indians from India, because they are essentially British sub- jects, and woutd hare every right arising therefrom,. Another reason for introducing Chinese Labour is equally cynical : The introduction of a little extraneous popula- tion of, say, 10,000 Chinese would create a feeling of rivalry among aborigines of the country, because they would argue then. ' If many of these people are coming, we shall not get work from the white men, even when we come to ask for it.' " Mr. F. \V. Pethick Lawrence, writing in the Reformers' Year Book, 1905, states : The mine owners talked also of Asiatic labour, and of closing down the mines in the event of their demands being refused. President Kruger's answer was a law providing that if the mines were not worked by the companies owning ttnni, it would be open to the State to step in. confiscate the mines, and work them itself. Thus the great weapon which the mine owners are able to use to-day so °flee- ' tively was taken away from them by the Boer Government, viz., their power to bring ruin upon the community at will by bringing business to a standstill. This law does not exist in the Trans- vaal under the British administration." And later, " One of the most interesting features of this ' Commission (Lord Miler's) was the expose, by Mr. Creswell, of the mineowners' prejudice against white labour. Questioned upon the subject he stated he knew that however financially successful it might be, the mineowners disliked it on political grounds. Proof of this statement was iemanded, and produced to the consternation of the mine- I owners on the Commission, in the shape of the following letter written by Mr. Percy Tarbutt, the ' Chairman of Directors of the Village Main Reef I Mine, of which Mr. Creswell was manager : " Dear Mr. Creswell,—With reference to your trial of white labour for surface work on the mines, I have con.ulted the Consolidated Gold Fields people, and one of the members of the board of the Village Haiti Reef has consulted Messrs. Werner, Belt and Co., and the feeling 1 seems to be on 3 of fear that, having a large nnmber I of white men employed on the Rand in the position of labourers, the same troubles will arise as are more prevalent in the Australian Colonies, viz : that the combination of the labouring classes will become so strong as to be able to more or less dictate not only on the qnestion of wages, but also 1 on political questions by the power of their votes when a Representatire Government is established. Yours sincerely. PERCY TARBUTT." The following sentence is significant : " Shortly after this Mr. Creswell's place was made too hot for him, and he tendered his resigna- tion, which was accepted." Mr. John Burns,speaking in the House of Commons, on 6th February, 1900, is reported to have said: I spent my Christmas holidays going through .the books of the Chartered Company's shareholders, and I find that nearly every one who has spoken in this debate here,—in the House of Lords and in the country—has his patriotism strengthened, and his speeches lengthened by the amount of his holding in the stock of the South Africa Company. . . . 350 generals and army officers, and newspaper pro- prietors by the yard &c." I have endeavoured, so far as possible, to give a clear and concise statement of the facts of the case as revealed by those in a position to know. The more one reads the " history ' of that deplorable war, the more one is disgusted with it. If Imperialism can, by any stretch of the imagination, be likened unto such a cowardly attack upon a homely, industrious nation of fartnersi"— as Mr. Chamberlain was once pleased

to call them—it is surely not an Imperialism to be proud of. Competition may be keen and brains may be bought at a pound per week, but neither the keenness of one nor the cheapness of the other should be allowed to inflict upon the good name of England anything which can be called dishonourable. The men who are prepared to hazard for the sake of gain, the honour of our Country are built of stuff which is not English. Their piles of gold may hide their blemishes for a time, but their names will, some day, be removed from amongst the pages of the respected ones and will find a resting place amongst the ashes of the sweaters and their dens. Society will be remodelled and a man's worth will bw reckoned, not by the length of his purse, but by his integrity and uprightness, and his desire to promote the best interests of humanity. Next week, I may have something further to sly, on other phases of " thought " which Nfr. Hughes has imhibad —and hurriedly rid himself of.
EDHUND OSBORNE.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHILD'S DEATH. Morphia Poisoning from Patent
div.p: WARRINGTON CHILD'S DEATH. Morphia Poisoning from Patent
Medicines.

The circumstances attending the death of Leonard Holloway, the eleveo-vveeks-old son of James Thomas Holloway, 14, Enville-street, ware enquired into by Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, at an inquest which was held at Warrington on Monday. It appears that the child was suffering from constipation. Dr. Braids WAS called in and prescribed for the child, and in addition Mr. Holloway ordered a few drops of a patent soothing syrup to be given to his son. The father's inatractions were carried oin and the child gradually became weaker and died on Friday. The Coroner read a letter from Dr. Braids, which stated that he found the child suffering from flatulence land constipation, and he recommended the necessary Iremedies. In the evening the child seemed to be in I pain, and some drops of soothing syrup were ordered to be given by the father of the child. He was called in early on Friday morning, and found the child suffering from morphia poisoning, and it died at 2.30. Mrs. Monks, from whom the syrup had been borrowed, had used the syrup for her own children. He had no doubt that the child died from the effects of morphia poison- ing. It was a very dangerous thing to givesnch a child morphia; he did not think any child ought to have it. The jury returned a verdict of Death from mis- adventure " due to morphia poisoning. The Coroner said he wished the Legislature would step in and say that all patent medicines should ba collected together and dumped into the sea.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

ORDER OF DRUIDS.—The quarterly Lodge night of the Penketh United Lodge, was held on Friday night last in the Infants School. There was a good muster of members, presided over by the N.G.A. J. Plumpton. A large amount of business was gone through and the election of °facers for the coming session proceeded with Bro. Plumption will retain his office for a further term, the Vice Chair being voted to Bro. Joseph Moores Bro. W. Whitfield resigned his post as Secretary, and Bro. Woods will fill the vacancy. Bro, FL J. Mainly was re-elected Treasurer. Much regret was expressed at the loss of Bro. Whitfield's services, as he has been a very hard working, and enthusiastic scribe. A feature of the evening was the presentation of an illuminated emblem of the Order to Bro. A. T Clay, for his energetic services in securing new member for the Lodge. The Grand 'Master of the Order, Bro D. Houghton made the presentation in a felicitous speech, and congratulated Bro. Clay on the active part he had taken in Lodge work since his inception. He had much pleasure in handing to him the beautiful emblem, and trusted he would long be spared to admire it. Bro. Clay responded in suitable terms, and urged on the members the need for each individual, to take an active and intelligent interest in Lodge affairs,and hoped that other members would do their best to earn an emblem under similar conditions, as the getting of new members was one of the best ways of helping the Lodge. LIBERAL CLI7L—The annual Christmas billiard handicap has just been concluded, after some interest- ing play. The ernes have been keenly contested, and several tight finishes testified to the judicious handi- capping. The prize winners were :—ist, Fred Dale ; 2nd, S. Tun.stall ; 3rd, Frank Houghton ; 4th H. Cheatham.

Volunteer Prize Distribution. The annual presentation of shooting prizes to the members of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (Prince of Wales's South Lancashire Regiment) took place on Thursday night in the new assembly room at the Drill Hall, Warrington. The commanding officer (Lieut.- Colonel Edelston) submitted an excellent report on the year's work aid said that the battalion numbered 1100 aim whieh was the largest number that he had ever known, except in 1901, when Volunteers were wanted for the war. Even then they had only thirty more. The increase during the past year was 100. He said that the report of the Brigadier-General (Sir Leslie Rundle) showed that the battalion was one of the finest in England. Subsequently the prizes were dis- tributed by Ur. R. Pierpoint, M.P., who was formerly a captain in the corps, to which he paid a high tribute. He said he only hoped that the governing body for the next five or ten years would do everything that could be done to forward the interests of the Volunteer corps, and make it even better than it was lat present. An excellent programme was submitted Iconsisting of humorous items, bayonet v. bayonet and bayonet v. sword exercises, and songs, and a highly 1 enjoyable evening was spent.
